script_body: The central market of Les Halles was Paris's pulsating lifeblood for nearly eight hundred years. In 1135, Louis VI set up a primitive market on land allotted by the Bishop of Paris, against a return of a third of its revenue. The marshy fields around it gave it its first name — Les Champeaux. In 1183, Philippe-Auguste replaced the open market with two stone buildings to shelter goods and vendors in bad weather, securing them with locks to prevent thefts. To raise the funds for the project, he confiscated the possessions of the Jews. The market became known as Les Halles — 'pour ce que chacun y allait,' for everyone went there — and the name stuck for eight centuries.

unverified_claims: Date 1135 vs 1137 — sources disagree. Book uses 1135, kept per editorial decision.

script_body: By the mid-19th century, France had entered the Industrial Age and iron was replacing stone. Impressed by Victor Baltard's newly built Gare de l'Est, Napoleon III commissioned him to rebuild the Les Halles market with a memorable instruction: 'Faites-moi des parapluies!' — make me umbrellas. Fourteen iron pavilions rose between 1851 and 1857, an artistic expression of the Industrial Revolution that stood for over a century. In 1969, the market was controversially transferred to Rungis south of Paris and the pavilions demolished. Only one of the fourteen survived, moved to the suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne. Sculptor Raymond Mason mourned: 'It was a place of bliss... the last vision of natural life in the City. It is now Paradise lost.' Social observer Louis Chevalier was blunter: 'The death of Les Halles has tolled the knell of Paris.'

script_body: Emile Zola dubbed Les Halles 'the belly of Paris,' a metaphor he used in 1873 for the title of one of his novels. For a year he haunted the market at all hours, recording the ever-changing hues of this gigantic digestive apparatus of the capital: dark bluish-grey metal structures against a light grey sky in wet weather, sheets of gold as the sun's rays penetrate on a fine day, glowing glass panes at sunset. He watched the robust porters — les forts des Halles, 'all nerves and muscles' — and descended into the undisclosable underground depths where the slaughter of fowl was carried out nightly, a place reeking of blood and pestilence and overrun by rats. This underworld was unknown to the bourgeois and the artist who, after a night at a cabaret, would drift to the market for onion soup and strong emotions.

script_body: The Dames des Halles — the market's notorious fishwives — occupied a unique position in Parisian society. On special occasions they were allowed into the King's Palace to pay their respects to the royal couple, and after a hearty meal they would return to Les Halles to pass on the latest Palace gossip. On 30 August 1608, one Femme Ladoucette wrote an astonishing letter to Marie de Medici, Henri IV's second wife. Having introduced herself as Dame des Halles 'from mother to daughter since Saint Louis,' she proceeded to complain about the King's philandering: a good fellow deep down, she wrote, but who 'fidgets at the sight of a coquette and scatters bastards around, although blessed with a most appetising Queen, so well conditioned to have little princes.' If the King wandered through Les Halles, she threatened, she would give him a sound thrashing for the love of her Queen. Femme Ladoucette received no scolding — instead she was promoted 'fournisseuse royale.'

script_body: With its ceaseless human tide, Les Halles was picked out for public executions and punishments from the 14th century onward. Decapitations were preceded by customary torture and followed by the mutilation of bodies. The King's pillory, the largest of them all, was a sizeable octagonal structure with a pointed roof and weathervane, somewhat resembling a chapel. The ground floor was often inhabited by the King's Great Executioner, while the convicts were exposed in the tower above. The excited mob relished the spectacle, taunting exposed victims and pelting them with rubbish and litter. There were no gallows, however — the King conceding that the market was no place for bodies to be left rotting on a rope.

script_body: The Ile de la Cite was the first part of Paris to be settled, occupied by the Celtic tribe of the Parisii in the 3rd century BC, making it the original nucleus of the city. In the 3rd century AD, the Roman Emperor Julian established his seat on the island, on the site of today's Palais de Justice — it was here in 360 that he was proclaimed emperor by his own soldiers. In the 6th century, the Merovingian king Childebert made it the permanent home of the kings of France. And in the 13th century, the pious Louis IX built a private chapel adjoining the palace — la Chapelle Royale, now known as la Sainte-Chapelle — to house a piece of the Holy Cross and the Crown of Thorns he had bought from the last Emperor of Constantinople.

script_body: French haute couture was born not on the grand boulevards of the 8th arrondissement where it lives today, but right here in the 1st — in the second half of the 19th century. The world of fashion concentrated around Place Vendome and the Tuileries to serve Empress Eugenie and the ladies of the Napoleonic nobility. Its illustrious forerunner was Charles Worth, the Empress's English couturier — a fitting irony that the most French of industries was pioneered by an Englishman. The legendary Ritz hotel opened on Place Vendome catering predominantly to affluent English visitors, who also frequented the fabulous jewellery shops on rue de Castiglione and rue de la Paix. For their convenience, WH Smith opened a Parisian branch at no. 248 rue de Rivoli. It would take another century for haute couture's centre of gravity to shift westward to the 8th arrondissement.

script_body: The Pavillon de Flore was completed as part of Henri IV's Grande Galerie — the colossal 470-metre wing connecting the Louvre to the Palais des Tuileries along the Seine. The gallery met the Tuileries at right angles, with the elegant Pavillon de Flore marking the junction. The Pavillon de Marsan on the northern side of the Tuileries was added only later, at the time of Louis XIV.

script_body: In the 13th century, rue de la Ferronnerie — just steps from Les Halles — was the stronghold of the iron trade after which it was named: a narrow, congested street cluttered with blacksmiths' and ironmongers' stalls. It was still much the same on 14 May 1610 when the royal coach carrying Henri IV was held up in traffic on his way from the Louvre to the Arsenal near the Bastille, where his minister Sully was residing. The King was absorbed in a letter when a man named Ravaillac jumped onto the coach and stabbed him to death. Ravaillac was declared mentally deranged but was nevertheless sentenced to be drawn and quartered on Place de Grève — today's Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville — a sentence speedily carried out just thirteen days after the crime.

script_body: At no. 93 rue Saint-Honoré, an apothecary bore witness to two of France's most traumatic royal events across nearly two centuries. An apothecary was already trading here on 14 May 1610, when Henri IV was stabbed by Ravaillac on the neighbouring rue de la Ferronnerie. One hundred and eighty-three years later, on the day of Marie-Antoinette's execution on 16 October 1793, the successor apothecary at the same address closed his shop 'Au Bourdon d'Or' as a sign of mourning.

script_body: Henri IV's early amorous adventures had gained him the affectionate nickname 'le Vert Galant' — the amorous youth. But the charm faded as he grew older. The population resented the fact that he had at least eleven illegitimate children scattered throughout the kingdom, which all but plunged France into civil strife yet again. Furthermore, he had expressed his intention to marry his favourite mistress, Gabrielle d'Estrées — an outrage to the raison d'état. Only her premature death prevented this infamy. As Femme Ladoucette, a Dame des Halles, had expressed it in her letter to the Queen: in the kingdom of France, one separated the sheep from the goats. The assassination on rue de la Ferronnerie in 1610 was not the first attempt on the King's life — his scandalous personal conduct had made him many enemies.

The original house was later demolished and replaced by the one still standing today, where the composer Richard Wagner reportedly stayed in 1839.

script_body: Outside Saint-Eustache, the streets of rue du Jour, rue Montmartre and rue Montorgueil have retained the atmosphere of the old Les Halles market. Although trendy boutiques are gradually taking over, they have not yet ousted the colourful displays of food that spill into the streets — mainly on rue Montorgueil — ravishing the eye and delighting the palate. Nearby, at no. 6 rue Coquillère, Le Pied de Cochon has preserved its Belle Époque setting and still serves its famous onion soup.

script_body: The green bookstalls of the bouquinistes lining the quais near Pont Neuf are a remnant from the time when the bridge itself was a world of its own, crowded with strollers, pedlars, acrobats, prostitutes and riff-raff. When the bridge was cleaned up in the late 18th century, its hucksters spilled over to the quais, eventually settling into the book trade that survives today.

script_body: In 1298, the extravagant Philippe le Bel ordered the reconstruction of a new palace on the Île de la Cité — 'the most beautiful that anyone in France ever saw.' Its Great Hall has survived as today's Salle des Pas Perdus. In its medieval heyday, the hall consisted of two naves separated by eight pillars, with a black-and-white chequered floor and polychrome walls. A huge marble table served both for sumptuous Gargantuan meals and as a stage for mystery plays, farces and other entertainments. Horrific skins of ferocious animals hung from the vaulted ceilings, and nobody seemed to mind the barbaric goings-on literally next door in the Conciergerie prison. The statues of every king of France stood against the pillars, gloriously painted in azure and gold — 58 in all by 1618, when a fire burnt down the hall with all its contents. Henri III had used the last available space for his own statue.

script_body: With King Jean II le Bon held captive in England, the provost of merchants Étienne Marcel reckoned on English support and believed he could overthrow the monarchy. On 22 February 1358, the Dauphin — the future Charles V — was sitting with two of his counsellors in the palace on the Île de la Cité when Marcel's men erupted in and slew the counsellors before his very eyes. The gushing blood of the victims stained the Dauphin's clothes, an experience he was never going to forget. A prudent politician, deservedly known as 'le Sage,' he left the palace one night stealthily by way of the river and moved to the Hôtel de Saint-Pol in the Marais, then arranged a residence within the safer walls of the Louvre, where he spent time from 1368 on. The kings of France never returned to the island, and the premises were taken over by the parliament — then the kingdom's court of justice.

script_body: At no. 1 quai de l'Horloge stands the entrance to the Conciergerie — originally the seat of the governor of the King's palace, hence its name. It became a prison in 1391 and remained so until 1914. Not unlike a modern concierge supplementing his income, the Palace concierge profited from vendors who leased the many shops within the Palace walls. But the prison's reality was far darker. In the 15th century, passers-by could still hear the screams of tortured prisoners in the Tour Bonbec — the most westerly tower. The name 'bon-bec' (meaning 'prate' in the Middle Ages) probably alluded to the interrogations on the ground floor: a varied spectrum of torture methods was devised to make victims confess and denounce their accomplices. During a restoration in 1828, two oubliettes were found in the tower's basement, communicating with the river and spiked with iron points — needless to dwell on the fate of the prisoners.

script_body: Among the notorious prisoners of the Conciergerie were Ravaillac, the assassin of Henri IV; the mass poisoner La Marquise de Brinvilliers (1630-1676), who had eliminated the better part of her numerous household; and Cartouche (1693-1721), the most notorious bandit of his age and the terror of Paris. To be admitted into Cartouche's prestigious gang, a candidate had to prove himself an expert cutpurse. Candidates were made to practise on dummies covered with little bells until they could strip them clean without the slightest tinkling. All three prisoners awaited execution at the Conciergerie.

fact_check.notes: Cartouche (Louis Dominique Garthausen, 1693-1721) confirmed. Brinvilliers executed 1676 confirmed. All held at Conciergerie confirmed.

script_body: During the Revolution, the Conciergerie boasted an impressive list of illustrious prisoners awaiting their deaths. Madame Roland, who had supported the Revolution but sided with the Girondins at the wrong time. Marie-Antoinette, who occupied a dreary cell from 2 August to 16 October 1793, when she was taken to the guillotine on Place de la Révolution. Then Danton, Robespierre and Saint-Just were detained here in their turn — Danton and Robespierre occupying the cells adjacent to the Queen's. In all, some 2,780 victims of the Revolutionary Tribunal passed through the arcade entrance to the jeers of delighted tricoteuses huddled on the perron.

script_body: North of the Conciergerie's Gothic halls was a section of the prison leading to the dark cells, known as 'rue de Paris' — named after the Great Executioner, Monsieur de Paris. This post was held by seven successive generations of the Sanson family, from 1688 to 1847, transmitted from father to son. Shortly before the Revolution, Louis XVI had set his heart on improving their plight and granted Charles-Henri Sanson an annual fee of 16,000 pounds plus 2,000 crowns for the upkeep of the scaffold and pillory — never suspecting he would become his own executioner. Being a royalist, Charles-Henri had no desire to carry out that deed. On 15 August 1792 he was arrested as 'the despot's employee'; with each execution he would be dispatched from his cell to Place du Carrousel, where the guillotine stood, and afterwards taken back. When the guillotine began to work at full swing and his expert hand could not be dispensed with, he was released — but retired soon after executing his sovereign. His son Henri held the position during the Terror and beyond, until 1840. The film-maker Jean Renoir marvelled that his own grandfather — the painter's father, a tailor from Limoges — had known Henri's chief assistant during the Terror: a man who 'may have passed Voltaire and Benjamin Franklin in the street, heard Mozart play the harpsichord.' Old Renoir befriended the assistant, and as Jean Renoir observed: 'After all, they were two good workmen: one cut out cloth, the other cut off heads just as conscientiously.'

script_body: Place Vendôme sums up the switchback history of 19th-century France in a single column. Girardon's original equestrian statue of the Sun King was disposed of during the Revolution. Napoleon's Colonne d'Austerlitz replaced it in 1810. With the Restoration, it was swapped for an equestrian Henri IV, le Vert Galant. When the bourgeois Louis-Philippe took the throne, the Vert Galant was dispatched to the Pont-Neuf and a Napoleon in a frock coat was set up instead — which his nephew Napoleon III later substituted with an imperial Napoleon as a Roman Caesar. In 1871 the Commune, led by the painter Courbet, toppled the column to the sound of the Marseillaise as thousands of patriots cheered. The Emperor regained his lofty position the following year when the bourgeois National Assembly sent him back to the top. He has been dominating this mecca of luxury ever since.

script_body: Passage des Panoramas was the first place in Paris to be gaslit, in 1817 — a dazzling novelty that drew the fashionable set to promenade here. The passage took its name from two circular Panoramas installed at the site: vast painted canvases that transported spectators to bloody battlefields or peaceful foreign lands. The concept had been invented and patented by the Irish-born painter Robert Barker in 1787, and the Paris installations became the dernier cri. The passage also housed the elegant Café Véron and the pastry shop Félix, making it one of the highlights of early 19th-century Paris.

script_body: At no. 7 Boulevard Montmartre, the Théâtre des Variétés still stands — the stage where Hortense Schneider created a sensation with Offenbach's La Grande Duchesse de Gérolstein in 1867. The premiere coincided with the Universal Exposition, and the audience included Napoleon III, the Prince of Wales, the Emperor of Russia, and Bismarck. Schneider's box became known as 'the passage of princes.' Next door at no. 9, the Café des Variétés had been a stronghold of Parisian literati until 1870.

script_body: The Paris Stock Exchange stands on the site of the convent of Les Filles de Saint-Thomas, which was closed during the Revolution. In the nascent age of capitalism, Napoleon had the convent razed and replaced it with this shrine to commerce, designed to emulate a Greek temple. For nearly two centuries it served as the nerve centre of French finance — though women were barred from entering until 1967, when Article XI prohibiting their admittance was finally repealed.

script_body: The painting above the high altar of Notre-Dame-des-Victoires tells a story of royal gratitude. It shows the Holy Virgin seated on a cloud, with Louis XIII at her feet presenting a plan of the church — his thanks for divine help defeating his enemies. To the King's right, a man surrenders the keys of the defeated town of La Rochelle, visible in the background. To his left stands Richelieu, whose initiative it was to eliminate the Huguenots and who obtained their surrender at La Rochelle in 1628. The illustrious architect of the Invalides, Libéral Bruant, collaborated in the construction of this pilgrimage church.

script_body: Among the famous Parisians buried at Notre-Dame-des-Victoires was Louis XIV's court composer Lully, whose funeral monument can still be seen between two side chapels. But the church itself had a turbulent afterlife: it was looted and wrecked during the Revolution, then found an unlikely second use as the Paris stock exchange between 1796 and 1809, before the Bourse moved to its purpose-built temple on Place de la Bourse.

script_body: The Bibliothèque Nationale traces its origins to Charles V in the 14th century, when the king concentrated his ancestors' manuscripts in a tower of the Louvre. The collection was scattered during the Hundred Years' War but gathered again in the 16th century by Louis XII and especially by the humanistic François I. Over the centuries it grew relentlessly — swollen first by the Revolution, when a prodigious flow of books confiscated from the aristocracy and religious institutions poured in, and then by the 19th-century explosion of printing. By the late 20th century the institution held over 12 million books, 6 million engravings, 800,000 coins and medals, and 400,000 records.

12 million books
source_passage: This monumental institution was initiated by Charles V in the 14th century, when he concentrated his ancestors' manuscripts in the tower of the Louvre

script_body: In 1643, Cardinal Mazarin rented a property at 8 rue des Petits-Champs — the Hôtel Tubeuf — to keep close to Richelieu's Palais-Royal. Within two years he had acquired all the land extending north to the present rue Colbert, including a second mansion. He commissioned François Mansart to build a gallery between the two mansions to house his art collection, and then a separate wing for his library of 40,000 volumes — the most impressive in Europe. Mazarin had sent emissaries to every court and kingdom with orders to buy every book unavailable in Paris, acquiring between 30,000 and 35,000 volumes in less than ten years.

source_passage: In 1643 Mazarin rented a property at 8 rue des Petits-Champs, the Hétel Tubeuf

script_body: Two hidden arcades lie side by side here — the highlight of the 2nd arrondissement. The Galerie Vivienne, with its tasteful, arty boutiques and good bookshops, has a charming, antiquated feel. Next door, the Galerie Colbert has been renovated into a more formal, classical compound in true French style, enhanced by its pale pink stone. Both offer an ideal refuge on a wet day — a glimpse of the covered-passage culture that once defined Parisian shopping.

script_body: Square Louvois stands on the site of Paris's ninth opera house. On 13 February 1820, the Duc de Berry — younger son of the future Charles X — was stabbed at the royal doorway of the theatre by a Bonapartist saddler named Louvel, as part of a scheme to rid France of the House of Bourbon. The Duke died the following day. Louvel was caught and guillotined before he could do more harm, and the King ordered the opera house razed to obliterate the scene of the crime. Today a graceful fountain by Visconti stands in its place, its allegorical figures representing the four biggest rivers of France that bear feminine names — which explains why the Rhône is not among them.

script_body: Lully actually lived nearby, in the corner house at nos. 45 rue des Petits-Champs and 47 rue Sainte-Anne. Its listed façade is decorated with musical instruments and masks of Bacchantes and satyrs — a fitting home for the composer who dominated French music under Louis XIV. The street names around Square Louvois — Cherubini, Rameau and Lully — are the only reminders of the neighbourhood's lyrical past.

script_body: At no. 6 rue Rameau, at the beginning of the 19th century, lived the idolized tenor Adolphe Nourrit, who premiered all the masterpieces of his time — the works of Rossini and Meyerbeer among them. During a performance of Halévy's La Juive in Marseille, he suffered a vocal crisis that ended his career. Devastated, he threw himself from a window in Naples in 1839. He was only 37.

script_body: Nearby rue Chabanais, opened in 1776, was famous above all for the internationally renowned brothel at no. 12, which from 1878 to 1946 catered to the exclusive clientele of the Jockey Club on Boulevard des Italiens. Most of the crowned heads of Europe frequented this impeccably tasteful establishment, as did ministers and government leaders of the Third Republic. Their visits were discreetly described on official timetables as 'visit to the President of the Sénat.' The splendid furniture was dispersed at auction at Drouot on 8 May 1951.

script_body: Passage de Choiseul, built in 1825, was once imbued with a rich cultural life. At no. 23 stood a publishing house that brought the Parnasse poets to the world — Sully Prudhomme, Leconte de Lisle, Heredia and François Coppée — followed from 1864 by Paul Verlaine. A few years later Anatole France worked here as editor for roughly a decade. At no. 73, the stage door to the winter Bouffes Parisiens still stands, where Jacques Offenbach, then director of the theatre, could be seen walking through during the winter seasons of 1855 to 1863.

script_body: In the celebrated Drouant restaurant on the corner of 18 rue Gaillon, the Goncourt Prize — the most prestigious of French literary prizes — is awarded every third Monday of November. Charles Drouant came up to Paris from Alsace in 1880, one of many compatriots torn by the loss of their region to the Germans. His restaurant soon attracted artists and writers with its fresh oysters from Brittany, and Alphonse and Léon Daudet, Rodin, Renoir, and Edmond de Goncourt became regulars. On 10 December 1919, Léon Daudet brought Proust the letter announcing he had won the prize for À l'ombre des Jeunes Filles en fleurs — though by a narrow margin of six votes to four over Dorgelès's war novel Les Croix de Bois.

script_body: At no. 5 rue Daunou, the red neon sign of Harry's Bar still beckons from a quiet, deserted street. This was a favourite haunt of Hemingway, whose photograph hangs on the wall, and of his friend Fitzgerald, who would drop in from the Ritz just round the corner. Opened in 1911, Harry's New York Bar was the heart of American expatriate Paris in the 1920s — and the birthplace of the Bloody Mary cocktail, mixed here by bartender Fernand Petiot in 1921.

script_body: Rue de la Paix was once the site of the beautiful convent of the Capucines, closed during the Revolution and converted into a theatre. A popular funfair was held in its gardens and the famous Franconi moved his circus there. In 1806, Napoleon razed everything to make room for a glorious thoroughfare to honour his name, entrusting the project to his architects Percier and Fontaine. After his defeat in 1814, however, the street was renamed rue de la Paix to commemorate the Peace of Amiens.

script_body: At no. 7 was the house of Charles Frederick Worth, rightly claimed to be the first haute couture designer, who raised dressmaking from craft to art. When Worth arrived from England in 1845, aged 20, he had just 117 francs in his pocket and knew not a word of French. He had served seven years apprenticed to the drapers Swan and Edgar, and after 12 years of hard work in Paris opened his own house on rue de la Paix in 1858. His timing was perfect: this was the heyday of the glamorous Second Empire, where multitudes of social upstarts, ready to squander unlimited sums, accepted Worth's tyranny because they could not claim to be his social betters. The reign of the haute couture designer thus began.

script_body: The head office of Cartier is still at no. 13 rue de la Paix. The house was founded in 1847 by Louis-François Cartier, who until then had been working for another famous jeweller, Adolphe Picard. He first set up shop near the Palais-Royal, then moved to the fashionable Boulevard des Italiens, where his customers included the Empress Eugénie and Napoleon III's cousin, la Princesse Mathilde. In 1899 his grandson Louis moved to rue de la Paix, by then the centre of luxury of the capital. Cartier's international clientele included Edward VII of England, Alfonso XIII of Spain, and the Duchess of Windsor.

script_body: In 1892, the prosperous banker Paquin set up his wife at no. 5 rue de la Paix. Madame Jeanne Paquin was the first major woman couturier and also the first woman in fashion to be awarded the Légion d'honneur, in 1913. A prominent public figure, she chaired the fashion section of the 1900 Universal Exhibition. At its peak, 2,700 employees worked for her establishment, which was located above Robert's chemist shop — opened in 1820 by Dr Roberts, chemist and surgeon to the British Embassy, and now the sole reminder of the street's former glories among the travel agencies.

script_body: Rue Notre-Dame-de-Nazareth sits at the heart of one of Paris's lesser-known Jewish enclaves. When the Revolution broke out, only about 500 Jews lived in the entire capital — Charles VI had banished them in 1394. After emancipation, Jews returned in growing numbers. The synagogue was inaugurated in 1822, but faulty construction led James de Rothschild to fund the replacement you see today.

The watch-tower owes its survival to Victor Hugo, who in 1882 protested: 'Demolish the tower — no; the architect — yes!' The priory church boasts the first example of Gothic rib vaults in the capital.

script_body: After decades of hospital expansion took its toll on the historic buildings, a restoration initiative began in the late 1970s to save the old monument. The chapel, cloister, and formal French garden have been beautifully restored. A museum of the army's health service was added, celebrating the site's unique dual identity as a place of both devotion and healing.

script_body: The beauty of the Val-de-Grace was recognized from the very start. Germain Brice, in the first guidebook to Paris published in 1684, wrote: 'Foreigners here must agree that things in France can be made beautiful and regular like those one goes to admire in Italy.' It was a bold claim — that Paris could rival Rome — and the Val-de-Grace was his proof.

Published in 1684
Quote praising Val-de-Grace comparing France favorably to Italy

script_body: The 5th arrondissement has the longest history of any district in mainland Paris, stretching back to the Roman occupation of Gaul. When the growing population of the Ile de la Cite spilled onto the left bank, Roman villas appeared on the slopes of Mount Leucotitius — now the Montagne Sainte-Genevieve. A north-south road, the cardo, ran along what is now rue Saint-Jacques, while a secondary cardo followed today's Boulevard Saint-Michel. By the end of the second century, this was a desirable neighbourhood of luxury — archaeological finds including marble and polychrome mosaics from rue de la Harpe attest to this. The Romans built three bath complexes: the northern ones at Cluny, the eastern ones at what is now the College de France, and the southern ones near rue Gay-Lussac. An aqueduct ran all the way from the Rungis basin near present-day Orly airport to supply them with water.

Cardo ran along present-day rue Saint-Jacques
Three bath complexes at Cluny, College de France, rue Gay-Lussac
Aqueduct from Rungis basin
source_passage: Roman villas appeared on the slopes of Mount Leucotitius (now the Montagne Sainte-Genevieve)

script_body: In the 13th century, the Latin Quarter became the centre of learning for all of Western Europe. The first official reference to the Universitas Magistrorum et Scolarium Parisiensium dates from 1221. Initially it had no permanent home — teaching took place in the open air, on Place Maubert and mainly on rue de Fouarre nearby. Teachers stood on wooden trestles while students sat on their own fodder — 'fouarre' in old French — hence the street's name. Brawls and political agitation were so bad that in 1358 the Regent and future Charles V had the street barred with chains on both sides. Among the greatest thinkers who came to teach: Albert the Great, Thomas Aquinas, and Brunetto Latini, master of Dante. Dante himself came to study on rue de Fouarre in the early 14th century.

Fouarre means fodder
Dante studied on rue de Fouarre
source_passage: The first official written reference to the Universitas Magistrorum et Scolarium Parisiensium dates from 1221

script_body: In 1253, a college was founded by Robert, the chaplain and confessor of Saint Louis. Born to a humble family in the village of Sorbon in the Ardennes, he became so great a scholar that the King had him dine at his table. The college became the seat of the faculty of theology and was known as La Sorbonne, after the native village of its founder. Its expansion was so spectacular that it soon overshadowed other institutions and many foreigners still mistake it for the entire University of Paris.

Chaplain to Saint Louis
Named after village of Sorbon in Ardennes
source_passage: One such college was founded in 1253 by Robert, the chaplain and confessor of Saint Louis

script_body: The enterprising Richelieu, who had been a student and later became dean of the Sorbonne, undertook its renovation. He laid the cornerstone of its chapel in 1635, designed by architect Jacques Lemercier. However, Richelieu's project was purely architectural — little was done to reform the curriculum, which until the Revolution remained restricted to theology. The beautiful compound, the work of Lemercier and Le Brun, was given rough treatment by the anti-clerical Revolutionaries. It was entirely reconstructed and expanded in the 19th century, including faculties of science and letters, inaugurated in 1901 with murals by Puvis de Chavannes.

Puvis de Chavannes murals in Grand Amphitheatre

script_body: In May 1968, a wind of revolt blew across the planet. Students transformed the Latin Quarter into a battlefield — not from premeditated political motivation but from a vague discontent with capitalism, imperialism, consumerism, and bourgeois rigidity. 'L'imagination au pouvoir' was scribbled on many a wall. Barricades were erected on all main arteries, cobblestones were dug from ancient streets and hurled at riot police, trees along the boulevards were felled. By autumn, the riots had died out. But the State proceeded to dismantle and decentralize the University, scattering students across the Paris area into numbered compounds — Paris I through XIII. The Latin Quarter lost its old cobbled streets, replaced with dull asphalt, and the arrondissement was forever changed.
physical_cues: asphalted streets where cobblestones once were
key_claims: May 1968 student riots
Slogan L'imagination au pouvoir
University decentralized into Paris I through XIII
source_passage: in 1968, a wind of revolt blew across the planet, from the Latin Quarter to Prague

script_body: Napoleon restructured French higher education by founding the celebrated Grandes Ecoles — elite engineering schools outside the university framework. The most prestigious, the Ecole Polytechnique, trains France's top mathematicians and remains a military school. Its cadets, the celebrated 'X', take part in the 14 July parade down the Champs-Elysees. Until 1976, it was located in the heart of the Latin Quarter in the premises of the medieval College de Navarre on rue de la Montagne-Sainte-Genevieve. Its transfer to Palaiseau deprived the Quarter of some festive pomp — previously, on ceremonial occasions, cadets could be seen passing in their Napoleonic uniforms bearing slender swords.

Ecole Polytechnique most prestigious military school
Located at College de Navarre until 1976 transfer to Palaiseau

script_body: The medieval Latin Quarter was a world of scholarly mischief. Neighbourhood taverns and brothels supplied the rowdy student population with cheap wines fit to 'boil the potted heads of wolves.' This was the Quarter that Francois Villon roamed in the 15th century, and of which Rabelais gave a saucy account. Favourite pranks included placing fried turds in graduates' hoods, pinning fox-tails or hare's ears to students' buttocks, making dogs run about with pots tied to their tails, and harassing maidservants. The church was a special target among these roguish, anticlerical youths. In Rabelais' story, the hero Pantagruel comes to study in Paris and visits the world-renowned library of the Abbey of Saint-Victor, which on the eve of the Revolution contained nearly 40,000 volumes and over 20,000 manuscripts.

key_claims: Villon roamed medieval Latin Quarter
Rabelais' Pantagruel visits Saint-Victor library
source_passage: This was the Latin Quarter that Francois Villon roamed a century later and of which Rabelais gave a saucy account

script_body: When the Hundred Years' War broke out, the University — which had gradually lost its earlier privileges — sided with the English against the King of France and, later, against Jeanne d'Arc. Paris was in ruins, the territory of wolves, and the Montagne Sainte-Genevieve had become an 'annexe of Oxford.' In due course peace was restored and in 1437 the University submitted to the secular authority of Charles VII.

Against Jeanne d'Arc
Submitted to Charles VII in 1437
source_passage: the University sided with the English against the King of France and, later, against Jeanne d'Arc

script_body: Place Maubert — 'la Maube' — had been home to rowdy students and ruffians since the Middle Ages, a place of crime, vice, and public executions. Erasmus called it 'the cesspit of la Maube.' In the early 20th century it was frequented by terrifying 'Apaches' and hoodlums. In Down and Out in Paris and London, published in 1933, George Orwell described the neighbouring rue du Pot-de-Fer — where he lived at number 6 — as 'a ravine of tall, leprous houses, lurching towards one another in queer attitudes, as though they had all been frozen in the act of collapse.' Amidst destitute Arabs, Poles, and Italians, respectable French shopkeepers quietly piled up small fortunes.

script_body: In 451, Attila the Hun was at the gates of Paris with his army. The terrified population was ready to flee the left bank, but Genevieve bolstered their courage, prophesying that Paris would be spared. Though romanticized as a shepherdess in the 17th century, Genevieve was born in Nanterre to a well-to-do Roman father and a Greek mother. She led an ascetic life devoted to the poor and sick, performed miracles, and her prophecy came true. She became the patron saint of Paris. It was under her guidance — and through the influence of his wife Clotilde — that King Clovis converted to Christianity and made Paris his capital. The basilica of Saint-Pierre-Saint-Paul was built on this hilltop site, receiving in its crypt both Clovis, who died in 511, and Genevieve, who died in 512 aged 89.

Genevieve born in Nanterre

script_body: Genevieve's reliquary, fashioned around 630 by the famous Saint Eloi — patron of goldsmiths and later minister to King Dagobert I — was chiselled in gold and studded with gems. In times of floods, epidemics, and calamities, following a day of penitence and fasting, it would be carried in procession to Notre-Dame through streets decked with multicoloured drapery and strewn with flowers, to the continuous chiming of all the city's church bells. The story goes that during a raging epidemic in 1130, all were cured except three sceptics who would not prostrate themselves and therefore died. By 1725 there had been 114 such processions. In November 1793, the Revolution stripped the reliquary of its precious stones and sent it to the Mint. Genevieve's remains were burnt on Place de Greve.

114 processions by 1725
Reliquary stripped November 1793
source_passage: Genevieve's reliquary was fashioned in 630 by the famous Saint Eloi

script_body: In November 1793, the Revolution's anti-clerical fervour reached Saint Genevieve. Her reliquary was stripped of its precious stones and sent to the Mint to be melted down. Against all logic, the remains of Saint Genevieve — who had embodied precisely the same ideals as the Revolution, feeding the poor and defending Paris — were burnt on Place de Greve. In one fell swoop, the Revolution destroyed twelve hundred years of devotion. The wooden sculptures of the reliquary survived, though they lost their arms, and are now in the Louvre. In 1803, a fragment of the saint's sarcophagus was discovered in the crypt and placed in a new reliquary above the altar of Saint-Etienne-du-Mont, where it remains today.
key_claims: November 1793 reliquary stripped and melted
Wooden sculptures survive in Louvre
1803 sarcophagus fragment discovered
source_passage: In November 1793 the reliquary was stripped of its precious stones and sent to the Mint to be melted down

script_body: The Revolution swept away the great Abbey of Sainte-Genevieve, founded in the 7th century by monks who settled next to Genevieve's holy shrine. But vestiges survive, now part of the Lycee Henri IV: medieval vaults, kitchens, a refectory, a cloister, the grand staircase dating from the 18th century, and the dome of the abbey's magnificent library. The square church tower on rue Clovis is the only element remaining in its original position. The abbey was a great place of learning, closely bound with the medieval University — its abbot held the post of chancellor and presented diplomas to graduates.

medieval vaults visible through school gate

Square tower on rue Clovis only element in situ

script_body: The Italian campaigns of 1515 impressed upon Francois I the artistic and intellectual achievements of Italy compared to the fossilized University of Paris. In 1530, to counteract its dogmatic theology and propagate the humanistic ideal of the Renaissance, he founded the College de France next to the Sorbonne. First known as Le College des Trois Langues — Hebrew and Greek were taught alongside Latin — it was soon renamed the College du Roi. Lectures were given in French, a revolution in itself. Over the centuries, the number of chairs grew from the initial three to over 40, but its principles have never changed: it remains independent of the University and its lectures are still free and open to the public. Among its illustrious professors were the historian Michelet, Champollion who deciphered the Egyptian hieroglyphs, the physicist Ampere, and the philosopher Bergson.

script_body: In 1640, Louis XIII chose a pleasant area on the sunny side of the 5th arrondissement as the site for a royal botanic garden for medicinal herbs, as suggested by his physician Jean Herouard. The Jardin Royal des Plantes Medicinales gathered 1,800 different plants for medical students. For two centuries, scientists of world renown developed natural science here: Cuvier, the father of paleontology; Buffon, who devoted decades to his Histoire Naturelle; and many others — Thouin, Tournefort, Linne, Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, the Jussieu family — all now honoured in the surrounding street names.

script_body: At 5 rue de la Huchette sits one of Paris's most layered buildings. It was once a meeting-place of the Templars of the Rose Croix, then in 1772 taken over by the Freemasons who turned it into a secret lodge, complete with underground passages to the Chatelet and under the cloister of Saint-Severin. During the Revolution, it was requisitioned and used as a court of justice and prison. The most prominent players — Marat, Danton, Robespierre — were brought here for trial, and their effigies still decorate the walls.

script_body: In the late 1940s and 50s, the Caveau de la Huchette became a mecca of jazz. After the Nazi repression, jazz became the musical expression of the avant-garde. American legends performed here — Coleman Hawkins, Art Blakey, Lionel Hampton, and Memphis Slim. The vaulted cellar's intimate atmosphere was so inspiring that Liverpool's famous Cavern Club — the very venue where the Beatles would later be discovered — was modelled on it.

script_body: At number 23 rue de la Huchette sits a tiny theatre with a world record. Since 1957, Ionesco's absurdist masterpieces La Cantatrice Chauve (The Bald Soprano) and La Lecon (The Lesson) have been performed here continuously — the longest theatrical run ever recorded in Paris and indeed a Guinness World Record. The 1950s were a time of literary turmoil and avant-garde theatre in the Latin Quarter, and this intimate venue became a permanent shrine to the Theatre of the Absurd.

script_body: Rue de la Huchette was already famous in the 17th century for its roasts and for its cutpurses, as a 1652 verse by Berthod warned: 'Vers la rue de la Huchette / Mais prends bien garde a tes pochettes!' — round rue de la Huchette, watch out for your purse! The street remained disreputable into the 20th century. In the 1920s it boasted three brothels, the most famous being Le Panier Fleuri on the southeastern corner of rue Xavier-Privas. A laundry on the opposite corner served as a clandestine annexe where a client could choose from among three laundresses without jeopardizing his reputation.

script_body: The Ecole Normale Superieure was founded in 1794 to provide France with highly cultivated and competent teachers. The greatest scientists of France — those now commemorated in the street names of the arrondissement — numbered among its professors. Today it has expanded beyond the Latin Quarter and even to the provinces, but the premises on rue d'Ulm, south of the Place du Pantheon, remain the most prestigious.

Premises on rue d'Ulm most prestigious
source_passage: the Ecole Normale Superieure, founded in 1794 to provide the nation with highly cultivated and competent teachers

script_body: To the west of the Roman settlement, on what is now rue Racine, stood a semicircular amphitheatre overlooking the Seine. The imposing arena was the second largest in all of Gaul after that of Nimes. It faced east to take advantage of the natural east-facing slope and the setting sun, which lit up the podium, with the pastoral Bievre meandering through green meadows towards the Seine in the background.

script_body: In 1744, Louis XV fell gravely ill and vowed to build a new church for Saint Genevieve if he recovered, recalling how in the 5th century she had healed her countrymen. The clergy, seeing divine punishment for his debauchery, urged him to also end his affair with the Duchesse de Chateauroux, the last of four sisters he had seduced. The king recovered, promptly resumed his liaison, and would have forgotten the church entirely, but the monks of the Abbey of Sainte-Genevieve held him to his word. Architect Soufflot was commissioned to build the colossal edifice — 110 metres long, 84 metres wide, and 83 metres tall — crowning the levelled hilltop. But the venture ended in tragedy: ancient potters had riddled the subsoil with clay pits, making foundations treacherous. Soufflot was showered with accusations and died a broken man before his monument was completed.

script_body: The Pantheon's tenants were shuffled with grim political theater. When revolutionary orator Mirabeau fell into disgrace in 1794 — his secret dealings with the king exposed — his body was exhumed and thrown into a common grave. His vacant spot was given to Marat, who met the same fate in 1795. Voltaire and Rousseau were likewise ejected by the Royalists in 1815, only to regain their places when the Bourbon dynasty fell. They have since been joined by dozens of luminaries: Emile Zola, Bergson, Saint-Exupery, and Jean Jaures, all occupying the sizable crypt originally built for the monks of the abbey.

key_claims: Mirabeau exhumed 1794
Marat removed 1795
Voltaire and Rousseau ejected 1815

script_body: Throughout the 19th century, the Pantheon's identity swung wildly between church and secular temple with each change of regime. Napoleon restored it to God; Louis XVIII dedicated it to Saint Genevieve in 1822. But 'citizen' King Louis-Philippe returned it to the Nation and added the patriotic pediment still visible today. Napoleon III re-dedicated it to the holy Genevieve, before the Third Republic reclaimed it for patriotism. The Republic needed an emblematic hero and found one when Victor Hugo died in 1885. His funeral — starting at the Arc de Triomphe, with two to three million mourners — was grander even than Voltaire's procession. The inscription 'AUX GRANDS HOMMES LA PATRIE RECONNAISSANTE', alternately put up and taken down for a century, was finally restored for good.

key_claims: Hugo died 1885 funeral from Arc de Triomphe
Inscription alternately put up and taken down with regime changes
source_passage: the destiny of the Pantheon vacillated to accommodate her respective regimes

script_body: Francois Mitterrand used the Pantheon for a masterstroke of political symbolism after his 1981 election. With Beethoven's Ode to Joy performed by the Paris Orchestra under Daniel Barenboim, and the socialist rose as his emblem, he walked alone into the crypt to lay roses at the tombs of Jean Jaures, Jean Moulin, and Victor Schoelcher. Parisians thronged to the event. By 1988, when Jean Monnet's ashes were brought here, the patriotic surge had died to indifference. In March 1994, on Women's Day, Mitterrand suggested Marie Curie's remains be interred — the first woman granted this honour. The transfer took place in April 1995.

Jean Monnet 1988

script_body: Inside the otherwise stark temple, two works preserve the memory of Saint Genevieve. Puvis de Chavannes painted a monumental cycle depicting her as the protector of Paris — simplified forms and pale, fresco-like coloring that became hugely influential. Above, Antoine-Jean Gros's mural of her apotheosis decorates the dome, lightening the dim interior where the 42 lateral windows were walled up when the building was converted from church to mausoleum.

script_body: At 10 Place du Pantheon stands the Bibliotheque Sainte-Genevieve, repository of tens of thousands of volumes rescued from the abbey during the Revolution. Built during the reign of Louis-Philippe and designed by Henri Labrouste, it was the first public building in the city with an exposed iron frame — predating the railway stations and Les Halles. It stands on the site of the notorious College de Montaigu, founded in 1314 and infamous for its filth, harsh discipline, and academic brilliance. Rabelais called it the 'college de pouillerie' (squalor), yet Erasmus, Ignatius of Loyola, Calvin, and likely Rabelais himself all studied here.

script_body: Saint-Etienne-du-Mont boasts the only surviving rood screen in Paris — a magnificent chancel screen in flamboyant style dating to about 1530. The church was built in the late 15th century when the adjacent abbey church grew too small. Its interior is striking for its asymmetrical structure, the ornate 17th-century organ, and fabulous 16th- and 17th-century stained glass displayed in the cloister of the Chapelle des Catechismes.

script_body: Here lie the remains of Pascal and Racine, but more importantly, the relics of Saint Genevieve herself. They rest in a brass reliquary — a poor 19th-century substitute for the bejewelled original that vanished in the fury of the Revolution in 1793. The stone underneath was rescued from the abbey's crypt and is believed to be part of the Saint's original sarcophagus. On 6 September 1914, with Germans at the gates of Paris, Parisians thronged here to pray, just as they had faced the Huns 1500 years before. When the war ended, many returned to leave plaques of gratitude on the chapel walls.

script_body: Across rue Clovis, the Tour Clovis is the only remnant of the old abbey church of Sainte-Genevieve, which was abandoned, its Gothic style having gone out of fashion, torn down in 1790, and replaced by rue Clovis. The tower lost its spire in 1750 and is now enclosed within the prestigious Lycee Henri IV, founded after the Revolution. Its pupils included Alfred de Musset, Viollet-le-Duc, Baron Haussmann, and all the sons of Louis-Philippe. French schools being sealed to outsiders, you can only peep through the doorway to glimpse the lovely flower-filled courtyard and the abbey library, now the school dining room.

script_body: Place de la Contrescarpe was 'Apache territory' in Hemingway's day and since time immemorial the haunt of students and youths. Though the square itself was only created in 1852, this junction was always a rowdy crossroads — sedan-chair carriers, servants, and revelers headed to taverns beyond the city walls where untaxed wine was cheaper. The most famous tavern was La Pomme de Pin, mentioned by Rabelais and frequented by the Renaissance poets of La Pleiade who united to promote the French language. Despite the inscription at no. 1, the tavern actually stood at the corner of rue Mouffetard and rue Blainville.

script_body: Before the 15th century, the borough of Saint-Medard lay by the happy river Bievre, proud of its vineyards and bucolic surroundings. Prominent Parisians built country homes in these sunny parts. Then the butchers, dyers, and tanners came, ravaging the river into a nauseating stench — 'mouffettes' or 'moffettes' — possibly the origin of the name rue Mouffetard. With pollution came social havoc: hot-tempered butchers and rowdy youths fueled by cheap wine made brawls a daily occurrence. In the early 18th century, authorities stationed the gardes francaises at no. 36 to keep order.

script_body: On 1 May 1727, the virtuous deacon Francois de Paris died at age 36. Despite his high birth, he had refused the priesthood and led an ascetic life of self-mortification. An ardent Jansenist during Louis XIV's persecution, his death unleashed mass hysteria. For five years, the convulsionnaires gathered at his grave — predominantly women — prancing, barking, mewing, nailing themselves to crosses, swallowing blazing charcoal, having their tongues pierced, and begging for more. When alarmed authorities shut down the graveyard in January 1732, the fanatics simply moved to private quarters. Only the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1762 ended this 35-year frenzy, which the Marquis d'Argenson considered a greater political threat than 'English philosophy.'

script_body: Saint Medard lived in the 6th century as councillor to the Merovingian Kings. In the year 545, he crowned a fair and virtuous village girl with a garland of white roses and gave her a dowry of 25 pounds, starting the village tradition of the annual Fete des Rosieres — a celebration of chastity among the maidens. The church was built on the site of a 7th-century predecessor destroyed by the Norsemen in the 9th century, its remains only discovered in 1978.

script_body: A gem of Moorish architecture and a slice of North Africa, the Grande Mosquee de Paris was inaugurated in great pomp by President Doumergue in 1926, when France was anxious to honor her Muslim subjects for their contribution to the war effort. The best Moroccan artists and craftsmen decorated it with magnificent tiles and mosaics, walls draped in rich damask. The ceiling of its arcades was carved from Lebanese cedar, its Turkish baths panelled in marble. The patio, decked with rose beds and a marble fountain, still carries faint scents of Arabia. On Fridays, colorfully dressed Muslims gather at the main entrance on rue du Puits-de-l'Ermite.

script_body: Next to the main entrance on rue Buffon stands the spacious 18th-century hotel bought by Buffon in 1772 to serve as the director's residence. Thomas Jefferson was a dinner guest here several times and both admired Buffon — 'a man of extraordinary powers in conversation' — and was warily deferential. Buffon died here fulfilled and happy in 1788, at age 80, just in time to avoid the Revolution. Under his supervision and with Louis XVI's support, the gardens reached their peak, containing some 10,000 species of plants, a tropical glasshouse, the trunk of a 2,000-year-old sequoia, and a cedar of Lebanon brought by Jussieu in 1734.

script_body: On 9 July 1827, Charles X was offered a giraffe as a present from the Pasha of Egypt — the first giraffe to tread French soil. Named Zarafa, she was paraded through the streets on her way to the Jardin des Plantes, cheered by enthusiastic crowds. Over 600,000 Parisians jostled to see her. Paris was gripped by a giraffe craze — images appeared on brooches, combs, umbrellas, anything one could find. But in the terrible winter of 1870-71, when Prussians besieged Paris, starving citizens invaded the menagerie and devoured all its animals, along with the rats and cats of the capital.

script_body: Nobody believed the Roman arena really existed until the 1860s, when workmen building rue Monge stumbled upon it accidentally. Haussmann's remodelling was not to be hindered by such trifles: in 1870, two-thirds of the unearthed arena were demolished for new apartment blocks and an omnibus depot. The last third, dug up in 1883, was likewise marked for destruction, but Victor Hugo intervened. 'It is not possible,' he wrote, 'that Paris, the city of the future, should renounce the living proof that it was a city of the past.' What you see today is the original surviving section plus a 1918 reconstruction of the demolished portion.

script_body: Designed by Jean Nouvel and inaugurated at the end of 1987, the Institut du Monde Arabe marked a new era of Franco-Arab cultural collaboration. It was one of Mitterrand's triumphant 'Grands Projets' that drew crowds eager to experience the novelty — above all the roof restaurant, with its spectacular view over the Seine. The building's south facade features 240 photo-sensitive mechanical apertures inspired by Arabic mashrabiya screens, automatically adjusting to sunlight. Unlike the Tour d'Argent a short way downriver, its meals remain within the bounds of affordability.

script_body: The world-famous Tour d'Argent at 15 quai des Tournelles first opened in 1582 as a countrified inn, yet even then it was a gastronomic establishment favored by the court of Henri III. Legend has it the fork was first used in France here during the reign of Henri IV, when the restaurant reached its peak. The Revolution destroyed this symbol of lavish decadence, but once the turmoil passed, the feast resumed. Since 1913, it has been in the hands of the Terrail family. Guests enjoy both cuisine and a spectacular view of Notre-Dame.

script_body: At 39 rue Descartes, a dilapidated room on the third floor was the last home of Paul Verlaine. After attempting to shoot his former friend Arthur Rimbaud, he served time in jail, tried to return to Christianity, but absinthe won out and he sank into depravity. Verlaine shared his seedy room with a wretched companion, Eugenie Krantz, and died here on 8 January 1896.

script_body: On 2 September 1792, the three-day September Massacres began when the bloodthirsty mob stormed places of detention. The College des Bernardins, which had become a depot for convicts after the Chateau de la Tournelle grew too dilapidated, was falsely rumored to hold clergymen in disguise. The mob stormed the depot and assaulted its 73 occupants, who put up fierce resistance with their bare hands. All except three were slaughtered in a frenzy that swept through the prisons of Paris, killing over a thousand.

script_body: Most visitors to Saint-Germain-des-Pres seek out Sartre's chair at the Deux Magots, but his actual wartime hangout was the upstairs of the next-door Flore. During the Occupation, the Deux Magots was infested with Germans, so Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir decamped to the Flore, where the owner Monsieur Paul Boubal had placed a heating stove in the middle of the room. During the harsh winter of 1943-44, they huddled at separate little tables, Sartre working on Les Chemins de la liberte, de Beauvoir on Tous les hommes sont mortels. By the time passers-by sought them out after the war, they had already migrated elsewhere, notably to the bar of the Pont-Royal hotel on rue du Bac.

script_body: Decades before the existentialists, the Flore harboured a far darker chapter. In 1899, during the retrial of Alfred Dreyfus, the virulent anti-Semite Charles Maurras, along with Leon Daudet, founded the Action Francaise movement and magazine here. This far-right publication prepared the ground for collaboration with the Nazis four decades later. When Maurras was sentenced to life imprisonment for collaboration in 1945 and expelled from the Academie Francaise, he cried out: 'It is the revenge of Dreyfus!' — connecting the cafe's dark political birth to its bitter end.

script_body: The abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Pres began as a basilica in the late 6th century. A deed from December 6, 558 records Childebert, son of Clovis, declaring 'I have begun to build a church.' The Bishop of Paris, Saint Germain, urged Childebert to erect a sanctuary for Saint Vincent, the patron of wine-growers. A relic of Saint Vincent's tunic and a gold cross said to have belonged to King Solomon were laid in the new basilica. Saint Germain had it decorated with magnificent mosaics and topped with a gilded roof, glittering amidst peaceful meadows — earning it the nickname Saint-Germain-le-Dore. The church tower that still dominates the Place pierced the skies of Paris less than a century later, and on 21 April 1163, the completed church was consecrated by Pope Alexander III.

script_body: Three centuries after his death, Saint Germain reportedly defended his abbey against the Norsemen through supernatural intervention, as recorded by a monk named Abbon. One Danish brigand was tied to a chariot by the invisible Saint, then chased into hell by Death. Another lost his way on a turret and rolled off the steep roof. A third lost his sight when he turned his eyes toward the Saint's sepulchre, while a fourth was snatched away from above by the Saint's invisible hand. Abbon's testimony increased the prestige of Saint Germain as the patriot who fought back the invincible Dane.

script_body: When Paris was liberated, the entire neighbourhood of Saint-Germain blazed into freedom. Boris Vian and his friends celebrated with trumpet blasts through the small hours at the Tabou on rue Dauphine. Claude Luter brought his unbridled clarinet and Dixieland to the basement of Lorientais. Club Saint-Germain at 13 rue Saint-Benoit picked up the baton in 1948, hosting Charlie Parker, Coleman Hawkins, Duke Ellington and Miles Davis. Meanwhile, Juliette Greco, dressed in all-purpose black, became the spokeswoman of existentialist Saint-Germain, singing to lyrics by Sartre, Queneau and Prevert. A new generation of anti-establishment singer-poets — Georges Brassens, Jacques Brel, Leo Ferre — made their appearance in vaulted cabarets.

script_body: American expatriates flooded Saint-Germain in the 1920s, making good use of the favourable dollar exchange rate and breaking loose from Prohibition. The newly-wed Hemingways, arriving in December 1921, could enjoy a hearty meal at the Pre-aux-Clercs on the corner of rue Jacob and rue Bonaparte for just 6 francs. Natalie Barney's literary salon at 20 rue Jacob, with its charming ivy-overgrown courtyard, gathered the beautiful people in a mock Greek temple dubbed Le Temple de l'Amitie. Gertrude Stein opened her home at 27 rue de Fleurus to chosen writers, while Sylvia Beach published and sold their works through Shakespeare and Company at 12 rue de l'Odeon — including James Joyce's Ulysses in 1922.

script_body: When two Armenians named Pascal and Maliban began selling coffee at the Saint-Germain fair in 1672 for two and a half sous per cup, the beverage received a mixed reception. Princess La Palatine declared it smelt like the breath of the Archbishop of Paris. A Sicilian nobleman, Francesco Procopio dei Coltelli — known as Francois Procope — added the cultural dimension when around 1686 he opened the first Parisian cafe on rue des Fosses-Saint-Germain. When the Comedie-Francaise moved across the street in 1689, Le Procope became its antechamber. By 1723 the chronicler Mercier counted between 600 and 700 cafes in the capital.

script_body: The Procope was where Diderot and d'Alembert conceived the idea of the Encyclopedie, and where new ideas germinated that would bring about the fall of the Ancien Regime. Already in 1685, the head of police warned Louis XIV about 'gatherings of all sorts of people' in coffee houses. The King flooded them with spies, to which the philosophes responded by inventing a coded terminology: 'liberty' became Jeannette, 'religion' became Javotte, and God became Monsieur l'Etre. A century later the Procope became the stronghold of the Revolutionary intelligentsia — Danton, Camille Desmoulins, and Marat all gathered here. It is also believed that the Phrygian cap of the sans-culottes made its first appearance here, worn by Citizen Julien.

script_body: At number 9, the workshop of Tobias Schmidt — a German harpsichord maker, not a carpenter as sometimes claimed — was where in April 1792 the guillotine prototype was first tested on live sheep. Dr Joseph-Ignace Guillotin had proposed the humane decapitation device to the National Assembly in October 1789, telling them: 'The blade whistles, the head falls, the blood gushes forth — with my machine I shall make your heads topple off in a flash.' The actual machine was designed by Dr Antoine Louis and built by Schmidt. After the successful sheep experiment here, the machine was tried on corpses at Bicetre on April 17. By April 25, the first public execution took place on Place de Greve. The guillotine devoured indiscriminately — even Dr Guillotin himself was condemned to his own blade, spared only by the timely downfall of Robespierre.

script_body: At number 8, directly opposite the guillotine workshop, Marat published his incendiary paper L'Ami du Peuple. Despite its benign name, the paper advocated wholesale executions, demanding the heads of 270,000 enemies of the homeland. Marat and his companion Marie-Simone Evrard had sold all their possessions to fund the publication. On July 13, 1793, Charlotte Corday arrived from Caen, bought a carving knife at Palais-Royal for 2 francs, and stabbed Marat through the neck as he sat in his bathtub. Asked about her deed, she said: 'I have not killed a man but a ferocious beast.'

script_body: The statue of Danton at Carrefour de l'Odeon marks the site of his home at what used to be number 20 Cour du Commerce-Saint-Andre, before the opening of Boulevard Saint-Germain cut away the southern section of the passage. Danton had been living there since 1789 when, on March 30, 1794, police burst into his large first-floor flat with a warrant for his arrest. Six days later he stepped onto the guillotine. Across the street, Camille Desmoulins and his young wife Lucile had been living at Place de l'Odeon when emissaries of the Terror came for them on the same day. Both husband and wife ended up on the guillotine.

script_body: At 28 rue Mazarine, just steps from the passage, Jean-Francois Champollion made his breakthrough discovery on September 14, 1822, cracking the principle of deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs. He was studying reproductions of bas-reliefs from Abu Simbel when he realised he could read the names of pharaohs Ramses and Thutmose. He rushed to his brother crying 'I've got it!' before collapsing in a faint from exhaustion. Two weeks later he presented his findings to the Academy, launching the field of modern Egyptology.

A key figure in the Surrealist movement and an active member of the Resistance, Desnos was deported to Auschwitz, then Buchenwald, and finally to Theresienstadt (now Terezin in the Czech Republic), where he died of typhoid on June 8, 1945 — on the eve of the camp's liberation.

script_body: Place Saint-Michel is dominated by Davioud's fountain of muscular energy, erected to the glory of the archangel Michael who struck down the dragon. The monument makes amends for the demolition in 1781 of the 12th-century chapel of Saint-Michel, which stood across the river next to the Sainte-Chapelle. Cleverly, the fountain is no more than a facing on the side wall of the first house on the block — a device to create a grand gateway to Boulevard Saint-Michel without taking up any space.

script_body: At 20/22 rue de l'Hirondelle, a derelict building with a magnificent entrance door conceals a salamander sculpted in stone — the emblem of Francois I. Here the King built a splendid love-nest for his favourite, Anne de Pisseleu, Duchesse d'Etampes. Renowned as 'la plus belle des savants et la plus savante des belles' (the most beautiful of the learned and the most learned of the beautiful), she patronized the arts and meddled in public affairs. But when Francois I introduced Diane de Poitiers to court, a seven-year war between the two women began. After Francois I died in 1547, Anne was banished to the provinces and ordered to hand over her personal jewellery to her rival.

script_body: Through rue du Jardinet, three successive courtyards known as la Cour de Rohan unfold like nesting Chinese boxes. Each reveals new surprises: crooked paving, an ancient well, cascading creepers and rose bushes. The third courtyard is a painter's paradise with its jumble of balconies, terraces and windows of all shapes and sizes. Two trees stretch their slender trunks up from the shady courtyard, reaching for the sun and then spreading leafy branches above the roofs. Near the exit, terraces explode with rose bushes, ivy and honeysuckle climbing above a white cottage with bright blue shutters.

script_body: The Theatre de l'Odeon was inaugurated on April 9, 1782, on the grounds of the Prince de Conde's former palace. Louis XVI deliberately chose a spot near the Luxembourg Gardens so that his subjects would have a promenade before or after the show. He insisted the theatre be built in the purest Classical Greek style — the largest in the capital with 1,913 seats, and the first to be lit by oil lamps. The surrounding streets were named after France's great playwrights: Corneille and Moliere flanking the building, with Racine, Voltaire, Crebillon and Regnard fanning out on either side. Rue de l'Odeon itself was the first street in Paris to have pavements and gutters.

script_body: The Theatre Francais lasted only seven years before the Revolution tore it apart. Beaumarchais's Marriage of Figaro had itself helped light the fuse by questioning the social order. Actors faithful to the royal troupe were imprisoned and the theatre was shut down between 1793 and 1794. In 1797 it was renamed the Odeon after the musical theatre of ancient Greece. Then in 1799 it burnt down entirely and lay as an abandoned ruin for eight years. Restored by Chalgrin in 1807 under Napoleon's Empire, it was renamed after Empress Josephine. Partly damaged by another fire in 1818, it was again restored in 1819.

script_body: The Institut de France began as Cardinal Mazarin's College des Quatre-Nations, founded to educate noble students from four provinces defeated and annexed by France. The site was the long-disused Hotel de Nesle, opposite the Louvre. Louis Le Vau created a magnificent monument with a domed chapel housing Mazarin's tomb, framed by two curving wings overlooking the Seine. During the Revolution the premises became a prison where, ironically, Dr Guillotin — father of the guillotine — was himself detained. In 1805, the five academies previously housed in the Louvre were transferred here: the Academie Francaise, des Belles-Lettres, des Sciences, des Beaux-Arts, and des Sciences Morales et Politiques.

script_body: The Academie Francaise, founded by Richelieu in 1635, is a stronghold of conservatism whose 40 venerable members guard the French language. It waited 350 years before admitting its first woman, the writer Marguerite Yourcenar, in 1980. Throughout its history, the Academie has rejected nonconformists: La Fontaine, Beaumarchais, Balzac (rejected 4 times), and Emile Zola (24 times). Others spurned the honour: Descartes, Pascal, Diderot, Malraux, and de Gaulle. After World War II, Charles Maurras and Marechal Petain were expelled — a rare measure, since an Academicien is by definition 'immortal.'

script_body: The Institut de France stands on the site of the medieval Hotel de Nesle and its infamous tower. In 1308, Philippe le Bel bought the palace where his three sons — the future Louis X, Philippe V, and Charles IV — lived with their wives Marguerite, Jeanne, and Blanche de Bourgogne. The tower served for their amorous liaisons until their sister-in-law Isabelle, wife of Edward II of England, noticed three gentlemen wearing purses she had given the princesses as gifts. The ensuing scandal was horrific: two of the lovers were castrated, decapitated, and hanged by the armpits for birds of prey. Marguerite was suffocated between two mattresses by order of her husband Louis X.

script_body: Next to the Institut de France stands the Hotel de la Monnaie, the Paris Mint, stunningly beautiful from across the river when illuminated at night. It was the work of a yet-unknown young mason and son of a carpenter, Jacques-Denis Antoine, who won the competition for the best design in 1765. The first stone was laid in 1771. Built on the site of Mansart's Hotel Guenegaud — said to be the most splendid dwelling in the city — the new building replaced aristocratic splendour with Neoclassical civic grandeur. In this earlier setting, Boileau and Racine had given readings of their early works and Lully's opera Pomone was rehearsed before its opening.

script_body: At 12 rue de l'Odeon, Sylvia Beach opened Shakespeare and Company in 1921, across the street from her friend Adrienne Monnier's bookshop La Maison des Amis du Livre at number 7. Here the lost generation met: T.S. Eliot, Ezra Pound, Scott Fitzgerald, Hemingway, and James Joyce, whose Ulysses was first published here in 1922 thanks to Beach's faith and energy. During the Nazi Occupation, Beach was forced to close and in 1942 went into hiding at a students' hostel at 93 Boulevard Saint-Michel. This original Shakespeare and Company should not be confused with the current bookshop of the same name near Notre-Dame.

script_body: Rue Dauphine commemorates the Dauphin and future Louis XIII and was opened by Henri IV as a continuation of the Pont-Neuf and Place Dauphine. The Augustine monks protested the new street would encroach on their grounds, but Henri IV was a man of vision and refused to bend, saying he would use his guns to carry his project through if he had to. He argued the monks would draw greater income from houses along the new street than from their cabbage-beds. History proved him right: on the eve of the Revolution, their order was one of the wealthiest in the capital. Rue Dauphine became one of the most elegant arteries, especially after 1763 when it was the first to substitute oil lamps for candles.

script_body: You are standing before the oldest church in Paris, built between 990 and 1014 AD in the Romanesque style. Look carefully at the second chancel — those small columns are survivors from the original 6th-century basilica that honoured Saint Vincent, before Saint Germain took over as patron. In 1163, a larger choir was built to accommodate growing numbers of monks, along with a bell-tower and majestic portal. Pope Alexander III himself presided over the ceremony — and just weeks later, he would lay the cornerstone of Notre-Dame cathedral across the river.

script_body: On 2 September 1792, the abbey prison that once stood across Boulevard Saint-Germain became the site of one of the Revolution's bloodiest episodes. Rumours of a plot against 'the good people' of Paris were deliberately spread, bells were rung, pamphlets distributed. After a mock trial, 100 prisoners including many priests were executed on the first day. By the third day, hundreds had been killed at or near the junction of rue Bonaparte and rue de l'Abbaye, their bodies piled in the abbey gardens. The killers worked by torchlight through the night, then tried to erase all evidence, ordering prison concierges to wash away blood with water and vinegar.

key_claims: September Massacres 2-4 September 1792
Prison stood where Boulevard Saint-Germain now runs

script_body: The abbey of Saint-Germain was once a city within a city, home to about 10,000 people, its domains reaching into today's 15th arrondissement. It answered directly to the Pope, ensuring political independence. Its 13th-century chapel, designed by Pierre de Montreuil — the same architect behind Sainte-Chapelle — was destroyed during the Revolution. When 15,000 tons of gunpowder stored in the dining hall ignited alongside a huge stock of coal, the explosion and fire devoured nearly everything, including a library of 50,000 volumes. Yet miraculously, most of its 7,000 manuscripts survived, including Pascal's original Pensées.

script_body: On the eastern wall of the church, look for the spectacular enamelled sandstone portico affixed to the garden of Square Felix Desruelles. It was manufactured by the celebrated Sevres workshops for the 1900 Universal Exposition. During the Revolution, the church was used as a refinery for saltpetre, leaving it in sorry state. Victor Baltard undertook its restoration, while Hippolyte Flandrin contributed the murals you can see inside.

script_body: In January 1857, Delacroix was living in the artists' quarter of La Nouvelle-Athenes when he was finally elected to the Academie des Beaux-Arts — after seven rejections. Seriously ill with laryngitis, he needed to be closer to his murals at Saint-Sulpice. He found this apartment through his dealer Haro, though converting it into a studio was, as he wrote in his journal, 'the devil's own job.' His fierce Breton housekeeper Jenny Le Guillou moved with him and increasingly barred visitors, especially women. He died here in 1863 at the age of 65. On his first morning, he wrote: 'I awoke to find the sun shining in the most welcoming way on the houses opposite my window.'

script_body: Over fifty years after Delacroix's death, in 1929, prominent artists including Bonnard and Signac founded La Societe des amis de Delacroix to preserve his memory. They rented these dilapidated premises, had them restored, and began organizing temporary exhibitions. By 1963, the Society persuaded the State to purchase the premises and establish a permanent museum. Today the collection charts Delacroix's artistic development through drawings, sketches, studies, and personal documents.

script_body: This bewitching square is named after Abbot Egon de Furstemberg, who in 1691 reconstructed the abbey's brick-and-stone Renaissance palace. You are standing on the site of the palace's main courtyard, turned into a square in the 18th century. The bright pink house at numbers 6 and 8 was painted to look like brick — because real brick was very expensive — and served as stables and carriage sheds for the palace. Henry Miller described it differently: 'A deserted spot, bleak, spectral at night, containing in the centre four black trees; these four bare trees have the poetry of T.S. Eliot.'

script_body: At number 13 rue des Beaux-Arts stands L'Hotel, now a luxury establishment but in 1900 a run-down place with appalling plumbing called Hotel Alsace. It was here that Oscar Wilde, poverty-stricken and exiled from Britain, lived 'beyond his means' as he famously put it, and died on 30 November 1900. His room has been recreated and constitutes a second Parisian shrine for the brilliant exile. His grave lies in Pere-Lachaise cemetery across the city.

script_body: This narrow alley opened in the 16th century and, being in a remote and therefore safer area, became home to Paris's Huguenot community, earning the nickname 'Little Geneva.' In 1559, the first synod of the French Reformed Church was held here, attended by delegates of 72 churches. When the Huguenots convened again months later, police surprised them, but all except four managed to escape. Among these Protestant residents was architect Jean-Baptiste Androuet du Cerceau, builder of the Pont-Neuf and friend of Henri IV, who preferred 'to part with the friendship of the King, than to go to mass.'

script_body: At number 16 lived Adrienne Lecouvreur, one of the most idolized actresses of the Comedie-Francaise in the early 18th century. Among her famous lovers was Marechal Maurice de Saxe, hero of the battle of Fontenoy and great-grandfather of George Sand. Voltaire was among her close friends and was by her side on 20 March 1730 when she died. No one knew the exact cause — some said it was for love of the Marechal, others that she was poisoned by a rival.

script_body: At numbers 17-19, Balzac lived in 1826-1828 during the early days of his career, trying his hand at business ventures. He opened a printing house here which brought in no money, and handed it over to the son of his much older friend and mentor Madame de Berny, in whose hands the business fared much better. It was probably here that Stendhal's masterpiece Le Rouge et le Noir was first printed. Later, Delacroix painted some of his greatest works in this same building, including L'Entree des Croises a Constantinople.

script_body: At number 24, the great playwright Racine spent the last seven years of his life. He settled here at the age of 53 in poor health and out of favour with Louis XIV, partly because the King had lost interest in theatre and partly because Racine was a Jansenist at a time when they were outlawed. Unlike his rival Corneille who died in destitution, Racine had a spacious apartment, 14 servants, a carriage, two horses and a small post-chaise. Both he and his wife were devoted Christians; of their seven children, four intended to become nuns.
