source_passage: N° 19 opens on to a picturesque outdated arcade, overlooked by most contemporaries: la Galerie Véro-Dodat which will carry you nearly two centuries back. Its beautiful glass ceiling, its black-and-white chequered floor, its mahogany panelling, its brass framings and handles served as backdrop to the promenade of fair ladies in crinolines and gentlemen in tail-coats and top hats [...] when it opened in 1826. The arcade's gas lights created quite a sensation and prices of property rocketed. But somehow, Messieurs Véro and Dodat, the two charcutiers (pork butchers) who had built the arcade, went bankrupt. In 1836 the celebrated actress Rachel moved to the 3rd floor of n° 38. The ground floor of the house was occupied by the famous satirical paper Charivari, to which Daumier contributed his cartoons. It was in the Charivari that the word 'Impressionist' was first coined by a journalist called Leroy. He had borrowed it from Monet's painting Impression, soleil levant and applied it derogatorily to the entire group of painters [...]. With the age of the stagecoach, the Messageries Générales opened premises on rue du Bouloi, on the other side of the arcade. From then on, the place became a convenient shortcut for travellers and its magical spell was broken. The beau-monde migrated elsewhere. What is left is an oasis of nostalgia, charmingly antiquated shops, among them Robert Capia at n° 26, a world-renowned dealer in antique dolls.

script_body: François d'Aubusson, maréchal and Duc de La Feuillade, idolised his king. He decided to put up a statue of Louis XIV on his own property, at his own expense — covered all over in gold, adorned with His Majesty's court cloak, crowned with a laurel wreath. At his feet, four chained women represented his trampled enemies: Spain, Holland, Germany, Franche-Comté. This done, the preposterous Maréchal called on the genius of Jules Hardouin-Mansart to create a setting worthy of the object of his worship. The result was the elegant Place des Victoires. La Feuillade, by then the laughing stock of Paris, is said to have relieved the King when he finally gave up the ghost. The statue was melted down during the Revolution; Bosio replaced it during the Restoration — this time Louis XIV sits on a caracoling horse, dressed as a Roman emperor, but still wearing his wig.

physical_cues.cue: Bosio's equestrian statue of Louis XIV in the centre of the square — Sun King on a caracoling horse, dressed as a Roman emperor, but still in his wig

source_passage: Ahead is the Place des Victoires, more famous today for its designer shops than for the victories of the Sun King it commemorates. François d'Aubusson, Maréchal and Duc de La Feuillade, idolized his King and decided to put up a statue in his honour on his own property and at his own expense. The statue was all covered with gold and adorned with His Majesty's court cloak. Its head was disproportionately large, overpowering the rest of the body and decorated with a laurel wreath. On the pedestal, at his feet, four chained women embodied dramatically the King's trampled enemies — Spain, Holland, Germany and Franche-Comté. [...] he called upon the genius of Jules Hardouin-Mansart. The result was the elegant Place des Victoires [...]. La Feuillade, by then the laughing stock of Paris, is said to have relieved the King when he finally gave up the ghost! The statue was naturally melted down during the Revolution, but was replaced by another one during the Restoration. This time the sculptor Bosio seated the Sun King on a caracoling horse, dressed him up as a Roman emperor, but kept his wig!

script_body: When Richelieu built this palace, it was known as le Palais-Cardinal. He bequeathed it to Louis XIII, and after the king's death the royal family moved in. It sat conveniently close to Mazarin's home on neighbouring rue Neuve-des-Petits-Champs, so a door was fitted into the wall around the palace to facilitate his rendezvous with Anne of Austria. That door proved handy in 1650 during the princely revolt of the Fronde, when the Queen and her two sons — the future Louis XIV and Philippe d'Orléans — escaped to Saint-Germain-en-Laye through it.

physical_cues.cue: Gardens of the Palais-Royal — Venetian-touched arcaded enclosure, sleepy and provincial despite Buren's striped columns and weekend crowds

source_passage: When the palace was built for Richelieu it was known as le Palais-Cardinal. Richelieu bequeathed it to Louis XIII and after the latter's death the royal family moved in. It was conveniently situated close to Mazarin's home on the neighbouring rue Neuve-des-Petits-Champs. To facilitate his rendezvous with Anne of Austria, a door was fitted into the wall that surrounded the palace. It proved handy in 1650, during the princely revolt of the Fronde, when the Queen and her two sons, the future Louis XIV and Philippe d'Orléans, escaped to Saint-Germain-en-Laye.

script_body: The fifth Duc d'Orléans — Philippe, father of the future King Louis-Philippe — was in deep debt when he took over the Palais-Royal. He built the arcades and their shops, rented them out, turned the establishment into a profitable business. Gambling houses and brothels opened up too. His new line was not to the taste of his royal cousin: "Cousin," said Louis XVI disdainfully, "you have turned shop-keeper and no doubt we shall see you only on Sundays." Philippe had his revenge. In 1793 he joined the Revolution, sat in the Convention as "Philippe Égalité," and voted for the death of the king. The guillotine took charge of him too, only a few months later.

source_passage: His grandson Philippe, the Fifth Duc d'Orléans and father of the future King Louis-Philippe, was in deep debt when he took over the Palais-Royal. He therefore built the arcades and their shops which he rented out, turning the establishment into a profitable business. Gambling houses and brothels opened up too [...]. The Duke's new line of activities was not to the taste of Louis XVI: "Cousin," he said disdainfully, "you have turned shop-keeper and no doubt we shall see you only on Sundays." Philippe d'Orléans would have his revenge: in 1793, having sided with the Revolution, he became member of the Convention under the name of Philippe Égalité and voted for the death of his royal cousin [...]. The guillotine, however, took charge of him too, only a few months later.

script_body: Among the shops of the newly-converted Palais-Royal was a cutlery establishment at no. 177 Galerie de Valois, owned by Monsieur Badin. On 13 July 1793 Charlotte Corday walked in and bought the knife with which she stabbed Marat in his bathtub the same day.

script_body: At no. 161 rue Saint-Honoré stood the Café La Régence — the Mecca of chess players, according to Diderot's Neveu de Rameau. The chessboards were rented by the hour, more at night when a candle had to be fixed on either side. "Paris is the place in the world, and the Café de la Régence the place in Paris where the game is best played." No fiction: François-André Danican-Philidor — composer, co-founder of the Opéra-Comique, and world chess champion — took on the world's best players here simultaneously and beat them one by one. His Analyse du jeu des échecs, published in London when he was twenty-two, remains a classic. In 1794, a young Napoleon shared a wretched existence between a dump of a hotel on rue d'Aboukir and La Régence, where he spent hours moving pieces on a chessboard — rehearsing, in his way, for the strategic showdown soon to come.

source_passage: the celebrated café La Régence (on the site of the present n° 161 rue Saint-Honoré) was the Mecca of chess players. [...] The chessboards were rented by the hour and cost more at night when a candle had to be fixed on either side. "Paris is the place in the world, and the Café de la Régence the place in Paris where the game is best played," he tells us. [...] François André Danican-Philidor, composer and co-founder of the Opéra-Comique, and also world chess champion, would take on the world's best chess players simultaneously at La Régence, and beat them one by one mercilessly. His Analyse du jeu des échecs that he published in London when aged only 22, remains a classic. [...] In 1794 Napoleon, an excellent chess player too, shared a wretched existence between a dump of a hotel in today's rue d'Aboukir [...] and Café de La Régence where he spent hours moving pieces on a chessboard, rehearsing for the strategic showdown soon to come.

script_body: The Café de Chartres at 79–82 Galerie de Beaujolais once served a Monarchist set menu of vermicelle et poitrine de mouton aux haricots. Its descendant, Le Grand Véfour, has abandoned homely fare for one of the best kitchens in Paris — and was, for this reason, targeted by Leftists to be blown up in December 1983. Next door at no. 83, Le Véry created a sensation as the first Paris establishment to offer meals at fixed prices. Among its clientele was the painter Fragonard, who actually expired here while savouring a sorbet.

source_passage: Le Café de Chartres, at 79/82 Galerie de Beaujolais, another Monarchist stronghold, served a set menu of vermicelle et poitrine de mouton aux haricots. Today, its descendant Le Grand Véfour has abandoned homely fare: with its wealth of decorations and choice dishes it is one of the best restaurants in the capital, and as such was targeted by Leftists to be blown up in December 1983. At n° 83 Le Véry created a sensation when it first opened, being the first Parisian establishment to offer meals at fixed prices [...]. Among them was the illustrious painter Fragonard, who actually expired here while savouring a sorbet.

script_body: By the time Colette was living at 9 rue de Beaujolais, and Jean Cocteau at 36 rue de Montpensier, the Palais-Royal had assumed its present aspect of outdated serenity. "In the mornings," Colette wrote, "we went out for a breath of fresh air — cat, bulldog and me — on the garden chairs, uncomfortable armchairs of venerable age." She catalogued her nameless, silent fellow citizens: the elderly lady leaning on her stick, the gentleman cultivating little cacti on his window sill, the other gentleman in straw slippers on his morning walk, the earnest little boy who might one day lay a marble in the palm of your hand, the lady who might read you the ode she had written to Victor Hugo. Cocteau dropped in on her "en voisin" — as a neighbour — though he was more than that, a friend and admirer who called her "an ink fountain." To quote Cocteau once more, this was "la campagne en plein centre de Paris."

She goes on to describe its nameless, silent citizens who followed a code of mysterious mutual courtesy: the elderly lady leaning on her stick, the gentleman cultivating little cacti on his window sill [...]. Jean Cocteau [...] dropped in on Colette 'en voisin'. He was a friend and admirer who called her 'an ink fountain'. [...] "La campagne en plein centre de Paris," to quote Cocteau once more.

script_body: The Comédie-Française was built between 1786 and 1790 by Victor Louis, the architect of the Bordeaux theatre. The Comédiens-Français inaugurated it on 30 May 1799 with a double bill of Le Cid and L'École des Maris, starring the great Talma and the adulated Mlle Mars. Among the surviving traditions: the baton-beats announcing the curtain rise, the declamation of the Marseillaise on Bastille Day, and the celebration of Molière's death every February. That death happened just around the corner. On the corner of rue de Valois and rue Saint-Honoré, Richelieu had built Le Petit Cardinal for his palace. It was there, on 17 February 1673 at ten in the evening, that Molière — playing Argan in Le Malade Imaginaire — collapsed on stage and died of a heart attack.

source_passage: On your right is the home of the prestigious Comédie-Française, built between 1786 and 1790 by Victor Louis, the architect of the famous theatre of Bordeaux. [...] Their inauguration performance on 30 May 1799 was a double bill of Le Cid and L'École des Maris, starring the great Talma and the adulated Mlle Mars. [...] the baton beats announcing the curtain rise, the declamation of the Marseillaise on Bastille Day, and the celebration of Molière's death every February. [...] In the 17th century, another theatre stood on the corner of rue de Valois and rue Saint-Honoré, built by Richelieu for his palace and named Le Petit Cardinal. It was here that at 10 pm on 17 February 1673 Molière was acting the part of Argan, le Malade Imaginaire, when he collapsed on the stage and died of a heart attack.

script_body: The name Louvre is believed to have come from Lupara, or Lupera — because wolves lurked here. The kings of France kept their treasures in the original keep, as specified in Louis VIII's will, who bequeathed his son Louis IX all the gold and silver kept "in our tower in Paris near Saint-Thomas."

source_passage: The original Louvre was just the keep of the stronghold built by Philippe-Auguste in 1190, on the site of the present Cour Carrée. The name 'Louvre' is believed to have derived from Lupara or Lupera, because packs of wolves lurked here. The kings of France kept their treasures in this tower, as specified in Louis VIII's will, who left to his son, Louis IX, all the gold and silver kept 'in our tower in Paris near Saint-Thomas'.

script_body: Urged initially by the dynamic Minister of Culture André Malraux, the archaeological excavation of the medieval Louvre began in 1983. President Mitterrand, a lover of "grands projets," continued the scheme wholeheartedly. I.M. Pei's glass Pyramid — twenty-one metres high by thirty-four wide — crowned the new underground entrance, a scintillating diamond by night. Not everyone hailed it; some dismissed it as too avant-garde, others objected to its location on a historic site. Its supporters countered that its geometrical starkness and transparency blended harmoniously into the old environment. Either way, 5 million visitors swarmed in within the first six months of its April 1989 opening, beating every record. For the first time since François I, they could see vestiges of the medieval Louvre, known previously only from the illuminations of the Duc de Berry's Book of Hours.

source_passage: Urged initially by the dynamic Minister of Culture, André Malraux, the archaeological excavation of the medieval Louvre began in 1983 [...]. President François Mitterrand, a lover of 'grands projets' [...], continued with the scheme wholeheartedly. [...] Its new underground entrance in the centre of the Cour Napoléon provided an ingenious solution [...]. Pei's glass Pyramid was to top it, perfect in proportions (21m high by 34 wide), a scintillating diamond by night. [...] 5 million visitors swarmed into it within the first six months of its opening, in April 1989, beating all records. Apart from the sensational Pyramid, they could now see - for the first time since the reign of François I - vestiges of the medieval Louvre, which only the 14th-century illuminated manuscript, the Duc de Berry's Book of Hours [...], had brought to our attention occasionally.

script_body: At 228 rue de Rivoli is the discreet entrance to the Meurice, where Thackeray and Dickens once stayed and where a penniless George Orwell was worked to the bone as a plongeur — "the slave of the slave," as he puts it in Down and Out in London and Paris. He never names the hotel; it is "a vast, grandiose place with a classical façade, and at one side a little, dark doorway like a rat hole, which was the service entrance." The kitchens were the kingdom of hell: "stifling low-ceilinged inferno of a cellar, red-lit from the fires, and deafening with oaths and clanging of pots and pans." Only a double door separated the squalid scullery from the dining room. "There sat the customers in all their splendour and spotless table-cloths, bowls of flowers, mirrors and gilt cornices and painted cherubims; and here, just a few feet away we in our disgusting filth." A generation later, the German High Command of the Paris garrison took up residence at the lavish Meurice. One wonders whether any of them had read Down and Out.

source_passage: At n° 228 is the discreet entrance to the celebrated Meurice where Thackeray and Dickens once stayed and where penniless Orwell was worked to the bone as a plongeur, "the slave of the slave", as we learn in Down and Out in London and Paris. The hotel, which he omits to name, is "a vast, grandiose place with a classical façade, and at one side a little, dark doorway like a rat hole, which was the service entrance." The kitchens are the kingdom of hell: "stifling low-ceilinged inferno of a cellar, red-lit from the fires, and deafening with oaths and clanging of pots and pans." Only a double door separated the squalid scullery from the posh dining-room. "There sat the customers in all their splendour and spotless table-cloths, bowls of flowers, mirrors and gilt cornices and painted cherubims; and here, just a few feet away we in our disgusting filth." We wonder whether the German High Command of the Paris garrison who, during the last war, took up residence at the lavish Meurice had ever read George Orwell.

script_body: The house at no. 258 is crying out for repair, but was once the home of the great statesman Talleyrand — the only man to have wormed his way through all the shaky regimes of the time. He died here of old age on 17 May 1838, aged eighty-six. His mansion was said to be the most sumptuous palatial residence in the capital, overlooking the Tuileries.

script_body: In 1720 a manège — a riding school — was built here for young Louis XV, on what was then the edge of the Tuileries Gardens; rue de Rivoli did not yet exist. After Louis XV left for Versailles, the manège became a riding school for upper-class youths trained in fencing, dancing, and mathematics, as befitted the gentlemanly ideal. In the early Revolution the National Assembly sat here, followed by the Convention. It was on this exact site, on 21 September 1792, that Danton proclaimed the First Republic — and where, soon after, Louis XVI was brought to trial and sentenced to death.

source_passage: In 1720 a manège was built for young Louis XV on the site of n° 230, then the edge of the Tuileries Gardens (rue de Rivoli being opened only in 1808). With his departure for Versailles it became a riding school for upper class youths, who were meanwhile trained in fencing, dancing and mathematics as befitted the gentlemanly ideal of the time. In the early stages of the Revolution the National Assembly sat here, followed by the Convention. Thus it was here that the first Republic was proclaimed on 21 September 1792 by Danton and that Louis XVI was brought to trial and sentenced to death.

script_body: Frémiet's statue of Jeanne d'Arc stands in the centre of the square. Historically it should be a little further east: at 161 rue Saint-Honoré stood Charles V's Porte Saint-Honoré, where the Maiden arrived on 8 September 1429 from the village of Monceaulx — today's Monceau in the 17th arrondissement — at the head of twelve thousand men, hoping to take the city. Injured in action, she had to retreat. The statue has become a shrine for all stripes of French patriotic fervour — today especially the far-right gatherings every first of May.

script_body: Place Vendôme is French classical architecture at its most polished — and its switchback statue sums up nineteenth-century France in a single column. Girardon's original equestrian Louis XIV went in the Revolution. Napoleon's Colonne d'Austerlitz replaced it in 1810. With the Restoration came an equestrian Henri IV, le Vert Galant. Then Louis-Philippe ousted the Bourbons and dispatched the Vert Galant to the Pont-Neuf; a bourgeois Napoleon in frock coat and low hat went up instead. Napoleon III substituted an imperial Napoleon dressed as a Roman Caesar. In 1871 the Commune — led on the square by the painter Gustave Courbet — sang the Marseillaise and le Chant de la Patrie as thousands of patriots pulled the column down. The Emperor, however, regained his lofty position the following year, when the victorious bourgeois Versaillais sent him back to the top. He has been dominating this Mecca of luxury ever since.

physical_cues.cue: Napoleon in Roman Caesar guise on top of the Colonne d'Austerlitz at the centre of Place Vendôme

inline_foreign_phrases.gloss: Austerlitz Column — cast from melted-down enemy cannon
the bourgeois National Assembly that suppressed the Commune, sitting at Versailles

source_passage: Place Vendôme is a work of art in its own right, a masterpiece of French classical architecture. It also sums up in a nutshell the switchback history of 19th century France: Girardon's original equestrian statue of the Sun King having been disposed of during the Revolution, Napoleon's Colonne d'Austerlitz came to replace it in 1810. With the Restoration of the monarchy, it was replaced in its turn by the equestrian statue of Henri IV, le Vert Galant; but soon the bourgeois Orléanais Louis-Philippe was put on the throne of France, ousting definitively the Bourbon branch of the dynasty — the Vert Galant was dispatched to the Pont-Neuf and a bourgeois Napoleon in a frock coat and low hat was set up in its stead, to which his nephew Napoleon III substituted an imperial Napoleon in the guise of a Roman Caesar. But in 1871 the Commune, temporarily victorious on Place Vendôme and led by the enthusiastic painter Courbet, would have none of it - thousands of patriots struck up the Marseillaise and le Chant de la Patrie, to the sound of the triumphant fanfare, as the monument came tumbling down. The Emperor, however, regained his lofty position the following year, when the victorious bourgeois National Assembly of the Versaillais sent him back to the top of the column.

script_body: The legendary Ritz opened on Place Vendôme in 1898 as the first hotel in Paris to install private bathtubs. It was the headquarters of the golden couple, the Fitzgeralds, through the 1920s — they made it their home but moved about Paris for the fun. Hemingway, by contrast, could only afford to come for a drink at the bar. That drink is still a worthwhile experience. The Ritz has since adjusted to modern demands — a cordon bleu cooking school, a basement health club.

source_passage: the fabulous Place Vendôme and the legendary Ritz, the headquarters of the golden couple the Fitzgeralds in the 1920s. They made it their home, but moved about Paris for the fun. Hemingway, quite the reverse, could only afford to come for a drink at its bar, still a worthwhile experience. The Ritz has adjusted to modern demands and opened a cordon bleu school, and a health club in its basement. When it opened in 1898, it was the first hotel to install private bathtubs.

script_body: Saint-Roch — named after the man from Montpellier who dedicated his life to plague-victims in Italy and contracted the disease himself — took nearly a century to complete from the reign of Louis XIV for lack of funds. It would have taken much longer had the financier John Law not donated a hundred thousand pounds toward the finish — not for any spiritual motive, but to be appointed contrôleur général. To that end he also converted to Catholicism, receiving his first holy communion right here. Saint-Roch being the fashionable church of its day, many illustrious Parisians lie buried in it: Pierre Corneille, Diderot, Madame Geoffrin — who had married here — and André Le Nôtre.

To that end he also converted to Catholicism, and it was at Saint-Roch that he received his first Holy Communion. script_body: The Arc du Carrousel's esplanade once held the sumptuous Hôtel de Rambouillet — red brick and white stone in the style of Henri IV and Louis XIII, on the now-vanished rue Saint-Thomas-du-Louvre. The Marquise de Rambouillet held her salon littéraire here in her chambre bleue — her blue-hung drawing room. All the literary set attended: Descartes, Scarron, Corneille, Madame de Sévigné, Madame de La Fayette, Mlle de Scudéry. The aristocracy too — Richelieu, the Prince de Condé. This is where the French language, hitherto as crude as the uncouth society that spoke it, was purified and polished; where conversation developed into an art, even an affectation; where French society finally shed its medieval remnants and was initiated into the urbane lifestyle that would dominate the next two centuries.

physical_cues.cue: Arc du Carrousel at the eastern end of the gardens — the Hôtel de Rambouillet stood on the now-vanished rue Saint-Thomas-du-Louvre, level with the entrance to the Palais-Royal

source_passage: originally these were sumptuous hôtels, erected in the immediate vicinity of the Louvre. The most famous was the Hôtel de Rambouillet, an elegant mansion of red brick and white stone, still in the style of Henri IV and Louis XIII. It stood on rue Saint-Thomas-du-Louvre, which ran parallel to the Tuileries Palace, level with the entrance to the Palais-Royal. Its fame was due to its landlady, la Marquise de Rambouillet, who in the 17th century held her prestigious salon littéraire in her chambre bleue. All the literary set attended her gatherings - Descartes, Scarron, Corneille, Madame de Sévigné, Madame de La Fayette, Mlle de Scudéry - and also the greatest aristocrats and statesmen, including Richelieu and Condé. This is where the French language, hitherto as crude as the manners of the uncouth society that spoke it, was purified and polished, where conversation developed into an art [...].

script_body: Catherine de Medici laid out the original Tuileries Gardens in 1564 in the Italian style, her native taste — and forbade access to the ramparts on the east side to protect her privacy in the small garden beside the palace. Henri IV had Jean Le Nôtre restore them after the wars of religion and planted mulberry trees, hoping to develop a French silk industry and break the Milanese monopoly. In 1664 Colbert commissioned Jean's grandson André to redesign the gardens west of the palace into a perfect jardin à la française. And in June 1662, Louis XIV — to celebrate the birth of his first son — held a spectacle of equestrian evolutions called a carousel. Fifteen thousand spectators packed the grandstand on the 2nd and 3rd. Dressed as a Roman Emperor, the Sun King caracoled and strutted, playing to his future favourite Louise de la Vallière. The name of the garden has stuck ever since — though today's visitor usually associates it with Napoleon's 1805 Arc du Carrousel at its eastern edge.

physical_cues.cue: Jardin du Carrousel — named for Louis XIV's 1662 equestrian celebration, not Napoleon's 1805 arch

source_passage: The original Carrousel and Tuileries Gardens were laid out for Catherine de Medici in 1564 by Pierre Le Nôtre and were Italian in style, to suit her native tastes. [...] The wars of religion left the gardens in a pitiful state and Henri IV had them restored by Jean Le Nôtre, the son of Pierre. [...] Driven also by economic considerations, he planted mulberry trees for the cultivation of silkworms, hoping to develop his own silk industry so as not to depend on expensive imports from Milan. [...] In 1664 André Le Nôtre, the grandson of Pierre, was commissioned by Louis XIV's Minister, Colbert, to redesign the gardens [...] a perfect model of a jardin à la française. [...] The birth of Louis XIV's first son in 1662 was no small event and Louis XIV meant to celebrate it with all the appropriate dazzling pomp, which included sumptuous equestrian evolutions known as carousel. 15,000 spectators gathered on the grandstand built for the occasion, to watch this brilliantly colourful spectacle on 2 and 3 June 1662. Dressed as a Roman Emperor, the Sun King took part in all the games of dexterity, caracoling and strutting about in order to impress his recent object of desire and future favourite, Louise de la Vallière. The impact of the carousel was such that the garden has been known as Le Jardin du Carrousel ever since.

script_body: The central pool was the departure point of the Revolutionary ceremony for the Supreme Being, orchestrated by a thickly powdered Robespierre dressed in blue, a bouquet of flowers in one hand, a torch in the other, haranguing the crowds. The master of ceremony, the painter David, fretted at the head of a red-painted float drawn by eight oxen, surmounted by a Liberty figure. Two thousand four hundred singers and a thousand musicians accompanied the procession into the Place de la Révolution — today's Concorde — where they skirted the guillotine before heading for the Champ-de-Mars. Meanwhile, a monster emerged from the pool in the shape of a pyramid, representing atheism, egoism, false modesty, discord, and ambition. Set alight, the monster was reduced to ashes, and Wisdom appeared in her splendour. All that survives of this inflamed idealism are some marble benches in a semicircle on either side of the entrance to the central alley — placed by the well-intentioned Robespierre for the aged participants. On 10 October 1794, the remains of J.J. Rousseau, wrapped in a gold-studded azure flag, were deposited by this same pool on their way from Ermenonville to the Panthéon. Robespierre was not present: the guillotine had disposed of him too, a couple of months before.

The master of ceremony, the painter David, fretted about at the head of a red-painted float drawn by eight oxen, surmounted by a Liberty figure. 2,400 singers and 1,000 musicians accompanied the huge procession into the Place de la Révolution (Concorde) [...]. Meanwhile a monster emerged from the pool in the shape of a pyramid (!), representing atheism, egoism, false modesty, discord and ambition. This time Robespierre was not present: the guillotine had disposed of him too, a couple of months before.

script_body: Today's Louvre is also a business venture. Make your way underground and past Pei's reversed pyramid, and you'll find — just beyond — yet another shopping arcade. This had been cautiously played down during the 1993 inauguration publicity. That the world of haute couture should transfer its fashion shows here from the makeshift structures on Cour Napoléon seems right enough — the area having been the birthplace of haute couture in the last century. But a shopping arcade communicating directly with the Louvre is another matter. "One day," as one visitor put it, "a MacDonald's will open under Notre-Dame."

physical_cues.cue: Reversed Pyramid in the Carrousel du Louvre underground — and just beyond it, the shopping arcade

source_passage: Today's Louvre is also a business venture as we found out some time later. Making our way underground, the transparent pyramid above our head displaying an ever-changing silver-grey sky, we proceeded in the direction of the Carrousel with enthusiastic anticipation to see Pei's more recent reversed Pyramid, when we discovered that just beyond it lay yet another shopping arcade! This had been cautiously played down during the inaugurational publicity campaign. That the world of haute couture should transfer its fashion shows here from the makeshift structures on Cour Napoléon only seemed right, the area having been the birthplace of haute couture in the last century. But a shopping arcade that communicates directly with the Louvre is a different matter. "One day a MacDonald's will open under Notre-Dame," someone next to me remarked.

script_body: For nearly two centuries the Paris stock exchange, La Bourse, has stood here as the financial centre of the capital. To honour the nascent capitalist era, Napoleon commissioned his architect Brongniart to endow the city with a new temple of finance, emulating those of ancient Greece. Napoleon never saw it finished: the monument was inaugurated in 1825, ten years after his downfall. Originally the Tribunal of Trade sat here too, but under the Second Empire it moved to Boulevard du Palais on the Île de la Cité. The stock exchange stayed, drawing French and foreign banks to the arrondissement and confirming its long-held role as the centre of financial transactions.

physical_cues.cue: Colonnaded façade of the Palais Brongniart, modelled on Greek temples

source_passage: For nearly two centuries, the Paris stock exchange, La Bourse, has stood imposingly in the heart of the 2nd arrondissement, marking it as the financial centre of the capital. To honour the nascent capitalist era, Napoleon commissioned his architect Brongniart to endow the city with a new temple of finance, emulating those of ancient Greece. Napoleon, however, was not to see the completed monument, which was inaugurated only in 1825, 10 years after his downfall. Originally, the Tribunal of Trade was also located here, but it was transferred to Boulevard du Palais on Ile de la Cité during the Second Empire. The stock exchange remained on the site and drew to the arrondissement a wide spectrum of financial establishments, both French and foreign, thus confirming the position the 2nd had long held as the centre of financial transactions and other communications.

script_body: In 1676 Louis XIV, fortified by his military victories, did away with the old city walls and laid out a tree-lined promenade in their place, emulating the Cour-la-Reine that his grandmother Marie de Médicis had planted along the Seine. These became the Grands Boulevards — the word comes from the German Bollwerk, meaning the top surface of a rampart. The arc ran from the Madeleine to the Bastille, a stretch that took a hundred years to complete and marked the northern boundary of Paris. In the 19th century the boulevards were the playground of the rising bourgeoisie and the heart of the modern capital, a fact symbolized by the first omnibus line, which plied between the Madeleine and the Bastille along their length.

source_passage: In 1676 Louis XIV, fortified by his military victories, did away with the walls and laid out a tree-lined promenade instead, emulating the Cour-la-Reine (now the 8th arr.), the promenade planted by his grandmother Marie de Medici along the Seine. These Grands Boulevards (the word comes from the German Bollwerk, meaning the top surface of a rampart) ran in a circular arc from the Madeleine to the Bastille, a long stretch that took a hundred years to complete and marked the northern boundary of Paris. [...] the playground of the new privileged classes and the heart of the modern capital, as symbolized by the first omnibus line, which plied along them between the Madeleine and the Bastille.

script_body: On 30 June 1878 the young Third Republic chose rue Saint-Denis for a national celebration, depicted in Monet's painting Rue Saint-Denis, now in the Musée des Beaux-Arts at Rouen — the street bursting with a riot of tricolours. The Republic needed a ritual to enforce its legitimacy, but was careful to avoid celebrating Bastille Day: the civil war of the Commune was only seven years past, and revolutionary feelings were still dangerous to rouse. The holiday was instead timed to coincide with the Universal Exhibition, which was bound to draw large crowds.

A national holiday was proclaimed to coincide with the Universal Exhibition, which was bound to draw large crowds.

script_body: This pretty square was the site of the Paris Opera House during the Restoration, and the scene of the assassination of the Duc de Berry, heir to the throne, on 13 February 1820, during a performance of the Carnival of Venice. The King ordered the theatre razed to the ground so as to eradicate the memory of the evil deed — and in doing so provided the congested arrondissement with its only open-air garden.

script_body: The Porte Saint-Denis had been the northern gateway to the capital since Charles V — a crenellated 14th-century construction complete with towers and drawbridge. In 1672 Louis XIV, confident that his spectacular victories meant Paris no longer needed defending, had the architect Blondel replace the defensive gate with the present monumental arch for the sole purpose of glorifying his person. Military function gave way to royal pageantry: the old fortification with its working drawbridge was dismantled and a trophy in stone took its place, a king's monument to a king whose armies, he believed, had made city walls obsolete.

source_passage: The Porte Saint-Denis at its northern end had been the gateway to the city since the reign of Charles V. In 1672, Louis XIV, confident that the city no longer needed to be defended after his spectacular victories, had Blondel replace the 14th-century gate, a crenellated construction complete with towers and drawbridge, with the present one for the sole purpose of glorifying his person.

script_body: Condemned prisoners on their way from the Grand-Châtelet prison to the gallows of Montfaucon would pass under this gate in a tumbril. At no. 237 rue Saint-Denis — just inside the walls — stood the wooden cross of the convent of the Filles-Dieu, and the tumbril would pause to let the prisoner kiss it. The convent's inmates, reformed prostitutes, would welcome the condemned man with a share of holy water, three morsels of bread and a glass of wine; they could even save his neck by consenting to marry him. One prisoner, offered rescue by a generous yet hideously ugly 'daughter of God', urged the hangman to proceed with his task and deliver him from a still worse fate. This may be the origin of the expression passer la corde au cou — 'to put someone's head in the noose', or to trap a man into marriage.

source_passage: Even those travelling to their deaths found solace here on their way to the gallows of Montfaucon (now 10th arr.). The tumbril carrying them from the prison of the Grand-Chatelet would pause to allow them to kiss the wooden cross of the convent of the Filles-Dieu (n°s 223-239). The convent's inmates, reformed prostitutes, would welcome them to a share of holy water, three morsels of bread and a glass of wine, and could even save their necks by consenting to marry them. It is said that one prisoner, who was offered rescue by a generous yet hideously ugly 'daughter of God', urged the hangman to proceed with his task and deliver him from a still worse fate. This may be the origin of the expression passer la corde au cou — 'to put someone's head in the noose', or to trap a man into marriage.

script_body: The Hôpital de la Trinité once extended between the present nos 164 and 142 rue Saint-Denis, set up originally to provide for belated travellers unable to enter the city after curfew. In 1402 the Confréres de la Passion were let a hall here and began to produce religious 'mysteries' — the life and feats of Jesus, probably amplifying the Old Testament stories enacted on the street during royal processions. So popular were these that the Hôpital de la Trinité became the capital's centre of entertainment and the birthplace of its theatre. In the 16th century it became a girls' orphanage, Les Enfants Bleus — 'the blue children', named for their blue uniforms; the girls were taught a craft from a very young age, generating a flourishing arts-and-crafts tradition that lasted until the Revolution.

script_body: In early 1408 Jean sans Peur, Duc de Bourgogne, was back in Paris after a year's absence following the assassination by his men of his cousin Philippe, Duc d'Orléans. Knowing he had many foes, he built himself a defence tower within the walls of his Hôtel and slept on the fourth and topmost floor, sandwiched between his squire, who slept on the third, and a squad of crossbowmen on the look-out on the crenellated roof. The tower still stands at no. 20 rue Étienne-Marcel — the only vestige of the Hôtel de Bourgogne, and Paris's only military medieval tower to have survived in its entirety, except for the 18th-century roof. The Spanish Ambassador persuaded Henri III to spare it while the rest of the property had been parcelled up by François I, hence the neighbouring rue Française, originally named Françoise. Jean sans Peur's room is reached by a spiral staircase, whose first section is in a square turret adjoining the tower and protected by an iron gate. At its top the proliferating branches of an oak tree are carved into the stone, symbolizing the power of the House of Bourgogne. A second iron gate once protected the last and narrower section of the staircase in a corbelled turret. In spite of these precautions, destiny caught up with Jean sans Peur, even though it took his assassin eleven years to get him. He was killed on the bridge of Montereau, south-east of Paris, at the confluence of the Seine and the Yonne. The murderer — in a perfectly balanced Shakespearean conclusion — was Tanguy du Châtel, head of the Armagnacs, the supporters of his own murdered cousin Philippe d'Orléans.

script_body: Further down and across the street, at no. 29 rue Étienne-Marcel, stood the Théâtre de l'Hôtel de Bourgogne, the first theatre of Paris. In 1548 the Confréres de la Passion, expelled from the Hôpital de la Trinité, took possession of the site. Hard times forced them to let the premises to three rival troupes who made history: Louis XIV's favoured Comédiens du Roi, who staged Racine; the Théâtre du Marais, which staged Corneille; and Molière's Théâtre Illustre. In 1680 the king ordered the three to merge and settle on the Left Bank. Only the Italian troupe was tolerated here — Harlequin, Colombine and Scaramouche — until in 1697 they derided Madame de Maintenon as La Fausse Prude and she had the theatre closed down. The Regent Philippe d'Orléans re-invited them in 1715, and in 1762 they obtained from the Opéra the privilege of creating a new genre in the same vein as the Opera Buffa, the Opéra-Comique. They stayed until 1783, when they moved to new premises on the Boulevard des Italiens, named after them; the Hôtel de Bourgogne was replaced by a leather market.

source_passage: Further down and across the street, at n° 29, was the Théatre de l'Hôtel de Bourgogne, the first theatre of Paris. The site is in the present 1st arrondissement, but for the convenience of sightseers and for historical coherence it is mentioned here. In 1548 the Confréres de la Passion were expelled from the Hopital de la Trinité and took possession of this site, vacated by François I. Hard times forced them to let the premises to different troupes, two of which went on to make history. The first one was the Comédiens du Roi who, through wily lobbying, enjoyed the patronage of Louis XIV, to the detriment of the rivalling Théatre du Marais, which staged Corneille's plays, and Molière's Théatre Illustre. The Hôtel de Bourgogne produced Racine's work. In 1680 Louis XIV, increasingly bent on imposing his authority, ordered the three troupes to merge into one and to settle on the Left Bank. The only other troupe he tolerated was the Italian one, which was allowed to take over the Hôtel de Bourgogne, delighting Parisians with the adventures of Harlequin, Colombine and Scaramouche. But when in 1697 the troupe derided Madame de Maintenon, thinly disguised as La Fausse Prude, she had the theatre closed down. When the fun-loving Regent, Philippe Duc d'Orléans succeeded Louis XIV in 1715, [...] The Italian troupe was invited again to the Hôtel de Bourgogne, where they entertained the audience with Marivaux's light-hearted comedies [...]. With the growing popularity of the Italian opera, in 1762 the troupe obtained from the Opéra the privilege of creating a new genre in the same vein as the Italian Opera Buffa, the Opéra-Comique [...]. The Italian troupe stayed here till 1783, when they moved to new premises just off the up-and-coming Boulevard des Italiens, named after them. The Hôtel de Bourgogne was replaced by a new leather market, more in keeping with the economic activities of the area.

script_body: Rue Montorgueil is a picturesque pedestrian artery lined with colourful food stalls. Since the fresh sea catch from the north used to arrive here, this became the fish section of the market of Les Halles, and the central oyster market of Paris until 1866. The sales office of the Société des Huîtres d'Étretat et de Dieppe was located at no. 61/63 from 1780 until the middle of the 19th century, called Au Rocher d'Étretat after the famous coastal landmark in Normandy. In the same century the street was a gourmet's mecca: Philippe at no. 54 and Le Rocher de Cancale at no. 59 until 1845, then across the street at no. 78. Balzac considered Le Rocher de Cancale 'the meeting place of the best society of Paris and the establishment which best honours French cuisine.' All the heroes of La Comédie Humaine dined there, and so did Balzac's contemporaries — Dumas Père, Eugène Sue and Théophile Gautier. The building at no. 78 still stands with the name of the restaurant engraved on its shabby façade.

Since the fresh sea catch from the north used to arrive here, this became the fish section of the market of Les Halles and also the central oyster market of Paris until 1866. The sales office of the Société des huitres [oysters] d'Étretat et de Dieppe was located at n° 61/63 from 1780 until the middle of the 19th century and was called Au Rocher d'Étretat, after the famous coastal landmark in Normandy. The town of Fécamp had its sales office further south on rue Tiquetonne. Rue de Montorgueil was also a gourmet's mecca in the last century, famous for such restaurants as Philippe at n° 54 and Le Rocher de Cancal at n° 59 until 1845, then across the street, at n° 78. Balzac considered Le Rocher de Cancal 'the meeting place of the best society of Paris and the establishment which best honours French cuisine.' All the heroes of La Comédie Humaine dined there, but also Balzac's contemporaries - Dumas Père, Eugène Sue and Théophile Gautier among others. The building still stands with the name of the restaurant engraved on the shabby facade.

script_body: It was in Madame Gourdan's glamorous establishment on this street — then called rue de la Comtesse d'Artois — that the notorious pimp Jean du Barry discovered the enticing Jeanne Bécu, Mademoiselle Lange by her trade name. Having set her up as procuress in the bordello Dupressoir on rue de Damiette, he threw her into the arms of the Duc de Richelieu, the Cardinal's great-nephew, who, hoping to promote his own interests, threw her into those of the King. To make her socially acceptable, Jean du Barry married her off to his brother, Comte Guillaume du Barry, who was compensated substantially for the deal and left for Toulouse, while the new Comtesse du Barry became the last of France's royal favourites. The people of France were infuriated by her prodigal spending on finery and on her sumptuous new mansion at Louveciennes. When the time came for revenge, a vindictive nation sent for her at Louveciennes and dispatched her to the guillotine.

Having set her up as procuress in the bordello Dupressoir on rue de Damiette, he threw her into the arms of the Duc de Richelieu, the Cardinal's great-nephew, who, hoping to promote his own interests, threw her into those of the King. [...] In order to make her socially acceptable, Jean du Barry married her off to his brother, Comte Guillaume du Barry, who was compensated substantially for the deal and left for Toulouse, while the new Comtesse du Barry became the last of France's royal favourites to the outrage of the scandalized court. [...] Outside the court, the people of France were infuriated by the Comtesse's prodigal spending, squandering the country's revenue on finery and on her sumptuous new mansion at Louveciennes. When the time came for revenge, a vindictive nation sent for her in her retreat at Louveciennes and dispatched her to the guillotine.

script_body: The narrow streets radiating from this place — rue du Nil, rue des Forges, rue de Damiette — cover the ground of the most notorious Cour des Miracles in Paris. By day the destitute bands who lived here spilled into the streets, metamorphosed into 'blind' or 'maimed' beggars, and preyed on passers-by. By night they vanished into the dead-end alleys, where they laid aside their crutches and 'miraculously' recovered their eyesight and missing limbs — hence the name. Victor Hugo's Notre-Dame de Paris brought worldwide notoriety to this one, calling it 'a gutter of vice and beggary, of vagrancy that spills over into the streets of the capital.' Hugo tampered with history, transposing this 17th-century den of thieves to the late Middle Ages to suit Romantic fancy. In 1667 Louis XIV ordered his police lieutenant Nicolas de La Reynie to clean up the hotbed of banditry. Its occupants put up heroic resistance; once defeated, many ended up in the galleys of the king's growing fleet — one way of tackling the problem of homelessness, which afflicted 40,000 souls, or one tenth of the population of Paris.

Victor Hugo's novel Notre-Dame de Paris brought worldwide notoriety to the Cour des Miracles of rue Neuve-Saint-Sauveur, 'a gutter of vice and beggary, of vagrancy that spills over into the streets of the capital [...].' Hugo, however, took the liberty of tampering with history by transposing this den of thieves from the 17th century to the late Middle Ages, to suit contemporary Romantic fancy. The rabble of the 'Cour des Miracles' made the streets of Paris so unsafe that in 1667 Louis XIV ordered his police lieutenant Nicolas de La Reynie to clean up this hotbed of banditry. This was no easy task, for its occupants put up a heroic resistance. Once defeated, many ended up in the galleys of the king's growing fleet; this was one way of tackling the problem of homelessness, which afflicted one tenth of the population of Paris or 40,000 souls. [...] By day they spilled out into the streets of Paris, metamorphosed into 'blind' or 'maimed' beggars, and preyed upon passers-by. By night they vanished into the neighbourhood's dead-end alleys, where they laid aside their crutches and 'miraculously' recovered their eyesight and missing limbs.

script_body: The proximity of the old city walls and of the central market of Les Halles had brought an influx of prostitutes to the neighbourhood, who left the mark of their trade in the old street names: rue Tire-Boudin — 'sausage-jack', now rue Marie-Stuart — and rue Gratte-Cul — 'bum-scraper', now rue Gaston Dussoubs.

source_passage: As Victor Hugo observed, the proximity of the city walls had brought an influx of prostitutes to the neighbourhood. They took up residence in the south-eastern section of the arrondissement, close to the abundant reservoir of clientele provided by the central market of Les Halles, and left the mark of their trade by way of street names: rue Tire-Boudin ('sausage-jack'; now Marie-Stuart), rue Gratte-Cul ('bum-scraper'; now Gaston Dussoubs)...

script_body: Towards the end of his life Pierre Corneille lived on rue de Cléry. After the death of his patron the Duc de Guise, he had to vacate the apartment in the Marais palace and petitioned the King for rooms in the artists' quarters in the Louvre. He couched the request in rhyme with all the customary florid flattery, but Louis XIV turned a deaf ear. Corneille's star was in decline and his plays had become outmoded: of all those he wrote here, Psyché alone proved a success — written to the music of Lully in collaboration with Quinault and Molière, it sealed Corneille's friendship with the latter. Louis XIV had meanwhile paired with the bigoted Madame de Maintenon, was losing interest in the theatre, and needed funds for the Spanish wars. He cut off altogether the pension of the playwright who had given him so much pleasure in his younger days. On 1 October 1684 Corneille died a pauper on rue d'Argenteuil, to which he had moved from rue de Cléry two years before. Six days later Psyché was revived at the Opéra, so great was its success.
source_passage: Towards the end of his life, Pierre Corneille lived in the rue de Cléry. After the death of his patron, the Duc de Guise, Corneille had to vacate the apartment given him in his patron's palace in the Marais and consequently solicited his sovereign to allow him to move to the artists' quarters in the Louvre. Although he took the trouble to couch his request in rhyme and pepper it with all the customary florid flattery, the King turned a deaf ear, a deplorable attitude as most of those granted accommodation in the Louvre were base courtiers and parasites. Corneille's star was in the decline and his plays had become outmoded: of all those he wrote on rue de Cléry, Psyché alone proved a success. Written to the music of Lully, in collaboration with Quinault and Molière, it sealed Corneille's friendship with the latter and offered him some comfort. Meanwhile, however, Louis XIV had paired with the bigoted Madame de Maintenon and was losing interest in the theatre. Moreover, the resumption of the Spanish wars meant that he was in need of substantial funds. He cut off altogether the pension of the playwright who had given him so much pleasure in his younger days. On 1 October 1684 Pierre Corneille died a pauper on rue d'Argenteuil (now between Avenue de l'Opéra and rue Saint-Honoré), to which he had moved from rue de Cléry two years before. Six days later, Psyché was taken up again at the Opéra, so great was its success.

script_body: Jeanne Poisson, unquestionably the street's most famously destined resident, was born to an unknown father roughly on the site of the present no. 29 rue de Cléry. Educated by the Farmer General Le Normant de Tournehem — the King's tax collector — she won the heart of Louis XV at the age of twenty-four and became the Marquise de Pompadour, to the indignation of the court and its scandalized ladies.

script_body: At no. 97 lived André Chénier, the greatest French poet of his time — although few read his poems. He has gone down in history as one of the most tragic figures of the Revolution: a friend of it at the start, he later condemned its excesses, notably the death sentence of Louis XVI, and siding with Charlotte Corday after her murder of Marat got him into further trouble. He was guillotined only two days before the downfall of Robespierre.

script_body: The corner of rue de Cléry and Boulevard Bonne-Nouvelle is the spot where, on 21 January 1793, the Baron de Batz and some of his supporters waited for the royal tumbril carrying Louis XVI from the Temple — where he had been sequestered — to the guillotine on Place de la Révolution by way of the Grands Boulevards. Batz had hoped to kidnap the King and save his head, but the plot failed, and two of his accomplices were massacred on the spot. Batz managed to escape and later devised a scheme to save Marie-Antoinette, then detained at the Conciergerie.

script_body: In 1874 the first Impressionist exhibition opened at no. 35 Boulevard des Capucines, within the framework of the Salon des Indépendants. The photographer Nadar had lent his painter friends his studio for the occasion. The press was less sympathetic: the works were described as 'black dribbles', 'slip-bang, swish-swash', done by 'hoaxers' or 'lunatics', the result of 'mental derangement'. It was all too much for the bourgeoisie of the nascent Third Republic.

script_body: On 31 July 1914, at around 9.30 pm, Jean Jaurès was having an animated dinner with fellow journalists from his paper L'Humanité, seated by an open window at La Chope du Croissant on the corner of rue du Croissant and rue Montmartre. Raoul Villain, a twenty-four-year-old nationalist, stood outside, drew the curtain, aimed at Jaurès and fired twice: Jaurès was dead for having opposed the war. The founder of the socialist paper — who had tried desperately to prevent the outbreak of the Great War — ironically became its first French victim. Villain benefited from the 'confusion of the time', in other words the prevailing nationalist hysteria, and was acquitted. Inside the café is displayed a copy of the next morning's front page of L'Humanité announcing the death of Jaurès, along with cuttings from other papers. Jaurès's table is there too, with a blood stain that never came off. Periodically, faithful disciples of Jean Jaurès gather here for dinner and even strike up the Internationale before breaking up.

source_passage: On 31 July 1914, at around 9.30 pm, Jean Jaurès was having an animated dinner with fellow journalists from his paper L'Humanité, seated by an open window at the the café La Chope du Croissant on the corner of rue du Croissant on your right. Raoul Villain, standing outside, drew the curtain, aimed at Jaurès and fired twice: Jaurès was dead for having opposed the war. Inside the café is displayed a copy of the next morning's front page of L'Humanité announcing the death of Jaurès, along with cuttings from other papers. Jean Jaures's table is there too, with a blood stain that never came off. Periodically, faithful disciples of Jean Jaurès gather here for dinner and even strike up the Internationale before breaking up. [...] Jean Jaurès, the founder of the socialist paper l'Humanité, was shot dead through the window of La Chope du Croissant, a hang-out of papermen on the corner of rue du Croissant and rue Montmartre, by Raoul Villain, a 24-year-old nationalist. Jaurès who had tried desperately to prevent the outbreak of the war, ironically, became its first French victim. His assassin benefited from the 'confusion of the time', in other words, from the prevailing nationalist hysteria, and was acquitted.

script_body: At no. 140/144 rue Montmartre, between rue Saint-Joseph and rue du Croissant, once stood the cemetery of Saint-Joseph, where Molière was buried on 21 February 1672. It took four days of tough negotiations and the King's intervention to persuade the recalcitrant clergy of Saint-Eustache in Les Halles, who regarded the theatrical profession as an insult to the Church, to agree to the burial at all. For a long time it was also thought erroneously that the fable writer La Fontaine had been buried here; there was confusion, too, as to the exact site of Molière's grave. When the Revolutionary authorities ordered the remains of the two illustrious writers to be exhumed and honoured elsewhere, other bones were dug up in their stead and eventually found their way to the cemetery of Père Lachaise, where they still receive undue homage. The cemetery was replaced by a market in 1806, and the market in turn by a building where, until 1914, several major newspapers were published. The façade still carries the engraved names of Le Journal du Soir and La France, supported by four female sculptures.

source_passage: At n° 140/144 on the right, between rue Saint-Joseph and rue du Croissant, was the cemetery of Saint-Joseph, where Molière was buried on 21 February 1672. It took four days of tough negotiations and the intervention of the King to persuade the recalcitrant clergy of Saint-Eustache, in Les Halles, who regarded the theatrical profession as an insult to the church, to agree to the burial. For a long time it was erroneously thought that the fable writer La Fontaine was also buried here. There was also confusion as to the exact site of Molière's grave. Consequently, when the Revolutionary authorities ordered the remains of the two illustrious writers to be exhumed and honoured elsewhere, other remains were dug up in their stead and eventually found their way to the cemetery of Père Lachaise (now in the 20th arr.), where they still receive undue homage. The cemetery was replaced by a market in 1806, and that in turn in 1882 by a building where, until 1914, several major newspapers were published - La Patrie, Le Radical, La Presse and L'Aurore. You can still see the building with the names of Le Journal du Soir and La France engraved on its facade, supported by four female sculptures.

script_body: On 13 January 1898 L'Aurore — printed in this building — ran on its front page the dramatic headline J'accuse!, followed by Émile Zola's open letter to the President of the Republic, Félix Faure, defending Alfred Dreyfus and directly accusing members of the General Staff. Three hundred thousand copies were hawked that day on the streets of Paris. Tried for libel and sentenced to one year's imprisonment and a heavy fine, Zola fled to England, like other French intellectuals who voiced unacceptable opinions. His manifesto polarized opinion on the Dreyfus case: there were mass riots and street duels fought with swords and pistols. Ten years later the fury had not abated. On the occasion of his pantheonization in June 1908 — the greatest posthumous honour bestowed on the Republic's heroes — his enemies marched through the streets shouting 'Spit on Zola! Death to Zola!', while Dreyfus himself was shot in the arm in an attempt on his life. On 30 September 1902 Zola's body had been found suffocated in his house, officially an accidental death, although many, including Zola's son, have always believed it was murder.

Tried for libel and sentenced to one year's imprisonment and a heavy fine, Zola fled to England, like other members of France's intelligentsia, before and after, who voiced unacceptable opinions (Voltaire, Victor Hugo, Charles de Gaulle...) But Zola's manifesto polarized French opinion on the Dreyfus case. There were mass riots and street duels fought with swords and pistols. Ten years later the fury against Zola had not abated and his enemies had not disarmed. Death to Zola !', while Dreyfus himself was shot in the arm in an attempt on his life. On 30 September 1902 Zola's body was found suffocated in his house, officially an accidental death, although many, including Zola's son, have always believed it was murder.

script_body: The Ile de la Cite is where Paris began. It was settled around 300 BC by a Celtic tribe called the Parisii, and in 52 BC was overrun by the Romans, who built a palace-fortress at the western end of the island. In the tenth century, the Frankish kings transformed this into a splendid palace, of which the Sainte-Chapelle and the Conciergerie prison survive today. At the other end of the island they erected the great cathedral of Notre-Dame. By the twelfth century the small island teemed with life, somehow accommodating twelve parishes plus numerous chapels and monasteries — too much for the monks at St-Magloire, who moved out in 1138 to quieter premises on the Right Bank.

script_body: It takes some imagination today to picture the medieval city, because most of it was erased in the nineteenth century by Baron Haussmann, Napoleon III's Prefet de la Seine — the equivalent of mayor of Paris. He displaced 25,000 people and destroyed ninety streets, which had, admittedly, become squalid and notoriously dangerous at night. In their place rose four imposing Neoclassical edifices, largely given over to housing the law and police. The few corners untouched by Haussmann include the tranquil square du Vert-Galant, place Dauphine, and the medieval streets rues Chanoinesse, des Ursins and de la Colombe, north of the cathedral.

script_body: The graceful, twelve-arched Pont-Neuf — despite its name, meaning New Bridge — is Paris's oldest surviving bridge. It was built by Henri IV, who is commemorated with a statue halfway across. Made of stone and free of the usual medieval complement of houses, it was a radical departure from previous structures, hence its name. Henri IV, one of the capital's first great town-planners, took much interest in the Pont-Neuf's progress and would sometimes come to inspect it, on one occasion delighting the workmen by taking a flying leap over an incomplete arch.

script_body: The square du Vert-Galant is enclosed within the triangular stern of the island, reached via steps leading down behind the statue of Henri IV on the Pont-Neuf. Vert-Galant — meaning a green or lusty gentleman — is a reference to the king's legendary amorous exploits, and he would no doubt have approved of this tranquil, tree-lined garden, a popular haunt of lovers. The prime spot to occupy is the knoll dotted with trees at the extreme point of the island. From here you can also hop onto one of the river boats that dock on the north side of the square.

script_body: On the eastern side of the Pont-Neuf, across the street from the Henri IV statue, red-brick seventeenth-century houses flank the entrance to place Dauphine, one of the city's most secluded and attractive squares. The traffic noise recedes, often replaced by nothing more intrusive than the gentle tap of boules being played in the shade of the chestnuts. At the eastern end is the hulking facade of the Palais de Justice, which swallowed up the palace that was home to the French kings until Etienne Marcel's bloody revolt in 1358 frightened them off to the greater security of the Louvre.

script_body: The only part of the Ile de la Cite's old palace that remains in its entirety is the Sainte-Chapelle, its fragile-looking spire soaring above the Palais buildings, its excessive height in relation to its length giving it the appearance of a lopped-off cathedral choir. Though damaged in the Revolution — when it was used as a flour warehouse — it was sensitively restored in the mid-nineteenth century, and remains one of the finest achievements of French High Gothic, renowned for its exquisite stained glass. It was built by Louis IX in 1242 to 1248 to house a collection of holy relics bought at an extortionate price — far more than the chapel itself cost — from the bankrupt Byzantine Empire. The relics, supposedly Christ's crown of thorns and fragments of the True Cross and a nail of the crucifixion, are now in Notre-Dame's treasury, displayed only on certain days, including Good Friday.

Though damaged in the Revolution, during which it was used as a flour warehouse, it was sensitively restored in the mid-nineteenth century, and remains one of the finest achievements of French High Gothic, renowned for its exquisite stained-glass windows. It was built by Louis IX in 1242–48 to house a collection of holy relics bought at an extortionate price – far more than it cost to build the Sainte-Chapelle – from the bankrupt Byzantium Empire. script_body: The Sainte-Chapelle actually consists of two chapels: the simple lower chapel was intended for the servants, and the upper chapel, reached via a spiral staircase, was reserved for the court. The upper chapel is dazzling — its walls made almost entirely of stained glass held up by powerful supports that the medieval builders cleverly crafted to appear delicate and fragile by dividing them into clusters of pencil-thin columns. When the sun streams through, the glowing blues and reds of the stained glass dapple the interior and you feel like you're surrounded by myriad brilliant butterflies.

script_body: There are 1,113 glass panels in the upper chapel, two-thirds of them original — the rest date from the nineteenth-century restoration. Together they tell virtually the entire story of the Bible: starting on the north side with Genesis, continuing with the Passion of Christ at the east end and the history of the Sainte-Chapelle relics on the south side, and ending with the Apocalypse in the rose window. The chapel is frequently used for classical concerts; tickets bought a day or so in advance avoid long queues.

script_body: The Conciergerie is one of the few remaining vestiges of the old medieval Palais de Justice and is Paris's oldest prison — where Marie-Antoinette and the leading figures of the Revolution were incarcerated before execution. Inside are several splendid, vaulted Gothic halls, including the Salle des Gens d'Armes, built in 1301 to 1315. The far end is separated off by an iron grille; during the Revolution this area was reserved for the pailleux, prisoners who couldn't afford to bribe a guard for their own cell and had to sleep on straw (paille).

script_body: Outside the Conciergerie stands the Tour de l'Horloge, a tower built around 1350, so called because it displayed Paris's first public clock. The ornate face, set against a background of fleur-de-lys, is flanked by statues representing Law and Justice, added in 1585. The clock tower's bell — which once rang out to mark special royal occasions, and sounded during the St Bartholomew's Day massacre — was melted down during the Commune.

script_body: East from the Conciergerie is place Lepine, named after the police boss who gave Paris's coppers their white truncheons and whistles. The police headquarters — known popularly as the Quai des Orfevres, as readers of Georges Simenon's Maigret novels will know — stands on one side of the square, though the police are set to move to new modern offices before long. Livening up the other side is an exuberant daily flower market, augmented by a chirruping bird market on Sundays.

script_body: A Gothic masterpiece, the Cathedrale de Notre-Dame rears up from the Ile de la Cite like a great ship moored by huge flying buttresses. It was built on the site of the Merovingian cathedral of St-Etienne, itself sited on the old Roman temple to Jupiter. Construction began in 1160 under the auspices of Bishop de Sully and was completed around 1345. The cathedral's seminaries became an ecclesiastical powerhouse, churning out six popes during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, though it later lost some of its pre-eminence to other sees, such as Rheims and St-Denis. The building fell into decline, and during the Revolution the frieze of Old Testament kings on the facade was damaged by enthusiasts who mistook them for the kings of France. Napoleon restored some of the cathedral's prestige, crowning himself emperor here in 1804 — though the walls were so dilapidated they had to be covered with drapes to provide a sufficiently grand backdrop.

script_body: In the 1820s Notre-Dame was given a much-needed restoration, largely thanks to a petition drawn up by Victor Hugo. Hugo had stirred public interest through his novel Notre-Dame de Paris, in which he lamented the building's sorry state — Gothic architecture was particularly favoured by Romantic novelists, who deemed the soaring naves of the great cathedrals singularly suited to sheltering tormented souls. The task was given to architect Viollet-le-Duc, who carried out an extensive and thorough renovation, some would say too thorough: he remade much of the statuary on the facade — the originals can be seen in the Musee National du Moyen Age — and added the steeple and the baleful-looking gargoyles. Viollet-le-Duc's parting contribution was a statue of himself among the angels lining the roof: it's the only one looking heavenwards.

script_body: Of the magnificent carvings over the portals, perhaps the most arresting is the scene over the central one showing the Day of Judgement. The lower frieze is a whirl of movement as the dead rise from their graves, while Christ presides above, sending those on his right to heaven and those on his left to hell. All around the arch peer out alert and mischievous-looking angels, said to be modelled on the cathedral choirboys of the time.

script_body: The left portal shows Mary being crowned by Christ, with scenes of her life in the lower friezes, while the right portal depicts the Virgin enthroned and, below, episodes from the life of St Anne — Mary's mother — and the life of Christ. These are masterfully put together, using visual devices and symbols to communicate more than just the bare-bones story. In the nativity scene, for example, the infant Christ is placed above Mary to show his elevated status, and lies on an altar rather than in a crib, symbolizing his future sacrifice.

script_body: If you climb the towers — access is round the side of the cathedral — you can see Viollet-le-Duc's gargoyles and angels up close, as well as the great thirteen-ton Emmanuel Bell in the south tower. One of the largest and oldest bells in Europe, the Emmanuel was forged in 1685 and spared during the 1789 Revolution, unlike Marie, the large bell in the north tower, which was destroyed and melted down. It is only rung at Christmas and other special occasions, or in times of mourning — such as the day after 9/11. The cathedral's other nine bells, which had become badly out of tune, were replaced in 2013.

script_body: Inside Notre-Dame, you're struck immediately by the dramatic contrast between the darkness of the nave and the light falling on the first great clustered pillars of the choir. It is the end walls of the transepts, nearly two-thirds glass and including two magnificent rose windows coloured in imperial purple, that admit all this light. These, the vaulting and the soaring shafts reaching to the springs of the vaults are all definite Gothic elements, while a strong influence of Romanesque remains in the stout round pillars of the nave and the general sense of four-squareness. The tresor is unlikely to appeal unless ornate nineteenth-century monstrances and chalices are your thing.

script_body: Notre-Dame, at the heart of Paris, is also the symbolic heart of France. Outside on the pavement by the cathedral's west door is a bronze star, known as kilometre zero, from where all main-road distances in France are calculated. The large windswept square in front of the cathedral, built by Haussmann in the 1860s, is the Parvis — from the word paradise — Notre-Dame. White paving blocks set into it trace the outlines of the small streets and buildings that stood here in medieval times.

script_body: On rue Chanoinesse, the cathedral school of Notre-Dame — forerunner of the Sorbonne — once flourished. Around the year 1200, one of the teachers was Peter Abelard, a philosophical whizz kid and cocker of snooks at establishment intellectuals. He was very popular with students but not with the authorities, who thought they caught a distinct whiff of heresy. Forced to leave the school, he set up shop on the Left Bank with his disciples, in effect founding the University of Paris. Less successful was the story of his love life. While living near rue Chanoinesse, he fell passionately in love with his landlord's niece, Heloise, and she with him. She gave birth to a baby, her uncle had Abelard castrated, and the story ended in convents, lifelong separation and lengthy correspondence. They were reunited in death, however, and lie side by side in Pere-Lachaise cemetery.

script_body: At the far end of the Parvis Notre-Dame is the entrance to the atmospherically lit crypte archeologique. The large excavated area holds the remains of the original cathedral, St-Etienne, plus vestiges of the streets and houses that once clustered around Notre-Dame — most are medieval, but some date as far back as Gallo-Roman times and include parts of a Roman hypocaust, an underfloor heating system.

poi_name: Memorial des Martyrs de la Deportation
script_body: At the eastern tip of the Ile de la Cite is the stark and moving symbolic tomb of the 200,000 French who died in Nazi concentration camps — among them Resistance fighters, Jews and forced labourers. The Memorial de la Deportation is barely visible above ground; stairs hardly shoulder-wide descend into a space like a prison yard, and off here is a stifling crypt where thousands of quartz pebbles represent the dead. Floor and ceiling are black, and it ends in a dark, raw hole, with a single naked bulb hanging in the middle. On either side are empty barred cells. Above the exit are the words "Pardonne. N'oublie pas" — Forgive. Do not forget. The little green park surrounding the memorial is more of a celebration of life and a popular hangout.

script_body: The Ile St-Louis is arguably the most romantic part of Paris. For centuries this was nothing but swampy pastureland, a haunt of lovers, duellists and miscreants on the run, until in the seventeenth century developer Christophe Marie chose to fill it with elegant mansions; by 1660 the island was transformed. Unlike its larger neighbour, the Ile St-Louis has no sights as such, save for a tiny museum at 6 quai d'Orleans devoted to the Romantic Polish poet Adam Mickiewicz. Inhabitants of the island even have their own name: Louisiens.

script_body: One of the most elegant mansions on Ile St-Louis, the Hotel Lauzun was built in 1657 by Versailles architect Le Vau. It has an intact interior, complete with splendid trompe l'oeil decorations. Its most famous inhabitant was the poet Baudelaire, who lived in a small apartment on the second floor from 1843 to 1845. He wrote much of Les Fleurs du mal here and hosted meetings of the Haschischins club, attended by bohemian writers and artists including Manet, Balzac and Delacroix — gatherings during which, as the name suggests, hashish was handed round, apparently in the form of a green jelly. Flutes of champagne are probably as heady as things get these days; the mansion is often used for government receptions, and is sometimes opened for guided tours.

It has an intact interior, complete with splendid trompe l'oeil decorations. Its most famous inhabitant was the poet Baudelaire who lived in a small apartment on the second floor from 1843 to 1845. He wrote much of Les Fleurs du mal here and hosted meetings of the Haschischins club, attended by bohemian writers and artists, including Manet, Balzac and Delacroix, and during which, as the name suggests, hashish was handed round – apparently in the form of a green jelly. Flutes of champagne are probably as heady as things get these days, as the mansion is often used for government receptions. It's also sometimes open for guided tours to the public – details are given in the "Visites conferences" section in Pariscope (see p.39).

script_body: More splendid still than the Hotel Lauzun is the Hotel Lambert, also built by Le Vau, at the tip of the island. In 2013 some of the building was destroyed by fire; fine frescoes by Eustache Le Sueur were lost, though many others were saved, including the galerie d'Hercule by Charles Le Brun, who painted the Galerie des Glaces at Versailles. Despite the damage, the mansion is still widely reckoned the most beautiful residence in Paris. Voltaire, a past inhabitant, thought it fit for a king. The building was bought by the Qatari royal family in 2007 for an estimated 80 million euros; their refurbishment plan, including a lift and underground car park, had to be scaled back after prominent historians and politicians protested.

script_body: Archaeological evidence suggests that a Celtic tribe called the Parisii first settled on the Île de la Cité in the middle of the River Seine during the 3rd century BC. The island was a secure settlement, having the Seine as a natural moat, but no defence was sufficient to protect the Celts from Roman invasion in 52 BC. There was relative peace between Romans and Celts, and the city, renamed Lutetia — meaning born of the waters — prospered.

script_body: In the Roman period the island was divided by a north–south axis: the east was residential and the centre of spiritual life, the west was administrative. Today the same divide exists, but the medieval cathedral Notre-Dame replaces the Roman temple to Jupiter. In the 19th century, many churches and the maze of medieval houses were demolished and the long straight streets of Haussmann were built.

script_body: The Marais was once below the flood plain of the Seine, and the name itself means the marshes. The first settlers were groups of Christians who built shrines, abbeys and convents and grew their own fruit and vegetables on the drained ground. The residential quarter only developed in the fourteenth century, once a huge city wall went up in the 1380s, ending at the Bastille fortress. The Marais is the quarter caught between that wall and the previous twelfth-century one.
